\textbf{Inverse Function Theorem:} $f:V\to\mathbb R^n$, $C^1$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, $a\in V$, $Df(a)$ invertible $\implies$
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $\exists$ open $U\ni a$, $W\ni f(a)$: $f|_U$ is 1-1 and $f(U)=W$.
\item $f^{-1}\in C^1$ on $W$, and $Df^{-1}(f(x))=[Df(x)]^{-1}$.
\end{itemize}

input.new_string:
\textbf{Implicit Function Theorem:} $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}$ open, $F\in C^1$, $F(a,b)=0$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$, $\det\frac{\partial(F_1,\dots,F_n)}{\partial(x_1,\dots,x_n)}(a,b)\neq0$ $\implies$
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $\exists$ open $W\subset\mathbb R^p$ containing $b$.
\item Unique $C^1$ function $g:W\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(b)=a$ and $F(g(t),t)=0$ $\forall t\in W$.
\end{itemize}
input.old_string: \textbf{Implicit Function Theorem:} $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}$ open, $F\in C^1$. If $F(a,b)=0$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\det\frac{\partial(F_1,\dots,F_n)}{\partial(x_1,\dots,x_n)}(a,b)\neq0$, then $\exists$ open $W\subset\mathbb R^p$ containing $b$ and unique $C^1$ function $g:W\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(b)=a$ and $F(g(t),t)=0$ $\forall t\in W$.

\textbf{FTC:} $F\in C^1[a,b]$ and $F'=f$ a.e. with $f\in\mathcal R$ $\implies\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$. Conversely, if $f\in\mathcal R[a,b]$ and $F(x)=\int_a^x f$, then $F$ is continuous and $F'(x)=f(x)$ a.e.

input.new_string:
\textbf{Differentiating Under Integral:} $f(x,y)$ continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$ $\implies$
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $F(y)=\int_a^b f(x,y)dx$ continuous on $[c,d]$.
\item If $f_y$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$, then $F'(y)=\int_a^b f_y(x,y)dx$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Uniform Boundedness + Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} $f_n$ uniformly bounded on $E$ ($\exists M:|f_n(x)|\le M$ $\forall n,x$) + $f_n\to f$ uniformly $\implies f$ bounded on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$ and each $f_n$ bounded on $E$, then $f$ is bounded on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Product of Uniformly Conv Functions:} $f_n\to f$, $g_n\to g$ uniformly on $E$, $f,g$ bounded on $E$ $\implies$ $f_ng_n\to fg$ uniformly on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Cesàro Mean:} If $b_k\to b$, then $\frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}\to b$. Equivalently, Stolz-Cesàro: if $c_n\to c$ and $a_n$ monotone or $d_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\to\infty$, then $\lim\frac{a_n}{d_n}=L\implies\lim\frac{\sum a_k}{\sum d_k}=L$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Arith. Mean Conv:} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ bounded $\implies$ $\frac{f_1+\dots+f_n}{n}\to f$ uniformly on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Differentiability:}

\textbf{Distance Between Sets:} $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{\|x-y\|:x\in A,y\in B\}$. If $A,B$ are compact and disjoint, then $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Cross Product:} $x,y\in\mathbb R^3$: $x\times y\perp x$ and $x\times y\perp y$. $\|x\times y\|=\|x\|\|y\|\sin\theta$. $x\times(y\times z)=(x\cdot z)y-(x\cdot y)z$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Balls are Open/Closed:} Open ball $B_r(a)$ is open; closed ball $\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is closed. Shell $\{x:s\le\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is neither open nor closed.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Relatively Open/Closed of Subset:} If $C\subset E\subset\mathbb R^n$: (1) $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ relatively open in $E$. (2) $C$ relatively open in $E$ + $E$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Closure/Interior Monotonicity:} $A\subset B$ $\implies$ $\overline{A}\subset\overline{B}$ and $A^\circ\subset B^\circ$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Interior/Closure of Subsets:} If $U\subset E$ relatively open in $E$: (1) If $U\subset E^\circ$, then $U\cap\partial E=\varnothing$. (2) If $U\cap\partial E\neq\varnothing$, then $U\cap\partial U=U\cap\partial E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{$\overline{A\cap B}\neq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$ in general. $(A\cup B)^\circ\neq A^\circ\cup B^\circ$ in general.}\\

\textbf{$L^p$ Spaces:} $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. H\"older: $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Minkowski: $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties:} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Outer Measure $\Rightarrow$ Measurable:} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ is measurable $\iff$ $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ open $U\supset E$ with $m^*(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli Lemma:} $\sum m(\Omega_k)<\infty$ $\implies$ $x\in\Omega_k$ for infinitely many $k$ has measure zero (i.e., a.e. $x$ in only finitely many $\Omega_k$).\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral Properties:} If $f,g\in L^1(\Omega)$: linearity $\int(cf+g)=c\int f+\int g$; if $f\le g$ a.e. then $\int f\le\int g$; if $f=g$ a.e. then $\int f=\int g$. Also $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Integral:} $f_k\in L^1$, $f_k\to f$ a.e., $|f_k|\le g$ with $g\in L^1$ $\implies$ $f\in L^1$ and $\int f_k\to\int f$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e.:} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e. (set $\{f=\infty\}$ has measure zero).\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity/Measurability of Composite:} $f$ measurable, $g$ continuous $\implies$ $g\circ f$ measurable. $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ measurable $\iff$ each $f_j$ measurable. $f$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ measurable $\forall a$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Almost everywhere modification:} $f$ Lebesgue measurable, $g=f$ a.e. $\implies$ $g$ is Lebesgue measurable.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Measurable Functions:} $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ measurable, $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$.\\[-2pt]

\section*{7. Lebesgue Measure}
\textbf{Outer Measure $m^*$:} For $E\subset\mathbb R$, $m^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum|I_j|:\cup I_j\supset E,\ \{I_j\}$ countable open intervals\right\}$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Measurable (Carathéodory):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ is Lebesgue measurable $\iff$ $m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ $\forall A\subset\mathbb R$. Equivalently: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ open $U\supset E$ with $m^*(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Lebesgue Measure $m$:} $m(E)=m^*(E)$ for all measurable $E$. All open sets, closed sets, intervals, Borel sets are measurable. $\mathbb Q$, countable sets, null sets are measurable with $m(E)=0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Defs (Functions/Integral):}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $E\subset\mathbb R$ has measure zero ($m(E)=0$): $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ countable cover $\{I_j\}$ with $\sum|I_j|<\varepsilon$.
\item Almost everywhere (a.e.): property holds a.e. if the set where it fails has measure zero.
\item $f$ Lebesgue measurable: $\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $\{f>\alpha\}$ is measurable (equivalently $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$).
\item Lebesgue integral: $\int_E f=\sup\{\int_E\phi:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ simple}\}$.
\item $f\in L^1$: $|f|$ integrable ($\int|f|<\infty$). For $f$ possibly signed: $\int f=\int f^+-\int f^-$, defined when $\int|f|<\infty$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Null Sets:} Every countable set has measure zero. Finite/countable union of null sets is null. $m(E)=0\implies E$ is measurable.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Properties of Measure:} $E$ measurable $\implies$ $E^c$ measurable; countable unions/intersections of meas. sets are meas.; $m(\varnothing)=0$, $m((a,b))=b-a$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties:} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Positive series} $\sum a_k$, $a_k\ge0$:

\section*{Ch6. Infinite Series of Real Numbers}
\textbf{Defs:} $s_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k$. $\sum a_k$ converges to $s$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|s_n-s|<\varepsilon$. Diverges: $\{s_n\}$ has no limit. Abs conv: $\sum|a_k|<\infty$. Conditional: conv but not abs.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Divergence Test (6.5):} $a_k\not\to0\implies\sum a_k$ diverges.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Geometric (6.7):} $\sum_{k=0}^\infty x^k=\frac1{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$, diverges for $|x|\ge1$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Cauchy Criterion (6.8):} $\sum a_k$ conv $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:m\ge n\ge N\implies\sum_{k=n}^m a_k<\varepsilon$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Comparison (6.14):} $0\le a_k\le b_k$ for large $k$: $\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$; $\sum a_k=\infty\implies\sum b_k=\infty$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{LCT (6.16):} $L=\lim a_k/b_k$, $b_k>0$. $0<L<\infty$: same conv. $L=0$+$\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$. $L=\infty$+$\sum b_k=\infty\implies\sum a_k=\infty$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Integral Test (6.12):} $f\ge0$ decr on $[1,\infty)$. $\sum f(k)$ conv $\iff\int_1^\infty f<\infty$. $\sum1/k^p$ conv $\iff p>1$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Root Test (6.23):} $r=\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ratio Test (6.24):} $r=\lim|a_{k+1}/a_k|$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} $\sum k/e^k$ conv by ratio test ($r=1/e<1$). $\sum k^2/(k+1)$ diverges ($a_k\to\infty$). $\sum1/k^2$ conv ($p=2>1$). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond conv ($|a_k|=1/k$, abs diverges).\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Abs Conv (6.20):} Abs conv $\implies$conv (converse false). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond converges.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Rearrangements (6.27):} If $\sum a_k$ abs conv, every rearrangement $\to$ same sum. Cond conv $\implies$ can rearrange to any $x\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Abel's Formula (6.30):} $A_{n,m}=\sum_{k=m}^n a_k$. $\sum_{k=m}^n a_kb_k=A_{n,m}b_n-\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}A_{k,m}(b_{k+1}-b_k)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test (6.31):} $\sum a_k$ partial sums bounded + $b_k\downarrow0$ $\implies\sum a_kb_k$ converges.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Alt Series Test (6.32):} $a_k\downarrow0\implies\sum(-1)^ka_k$ converges.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Alt Series Error (6.38):} $a_k\downarrow0$, $s=\sum(-1)^ka_k$, $|s-s_n|\le a_{n+1}$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Integral Test Error (6.35):} $0\le\sum_{k=1}^n f(k)-\int_1^n f\le f(1)$. If $\sum f(k)$ conv: $0\le s-s_n+\int_n^\infty f\le f(n)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Logarithmic Test (6.42):} $p=\lim\frac{\log(1/|a_k|)}{\log k}$. $p>1\implies$abs conv; $p<1\implies$diverge.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Raabe's Test (6.43):} $|a_{k+1}/a_k|\le1-p/k+O(1/k)$ with $p>1\implies\sum a_k$ abs conv.

\section*{Ch7. Infinite Series of Functions}
\textbf{Defs:}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $f_n\to f$ ptwise: $\forall x\in E$, $\lim f_n(x)=f(x)$.
\item $f_n\to f$ uniformly: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$. ($N$ depends only on $\varepsilon$.)
\item Radius of conv $R$: abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (7.9):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ cont at $x_0\in E$ $\implies f$ cont at $x_0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Integrability (7.10):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$, each integrable $\implies f$ integrable and $\int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform Boundedness + Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} $f_n$ uniformly bounded on $E$ ($\exists M:|f_n(x)|\le M$ $\forall n,x$) + $f_n\to f$ uniformly $\implies f$ bounded on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$ and each $f_n$ bounded on $E$, then $f$ is bounded on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Product of Uniformly Conv Functions:} If: (1) $f_n\to f$, $g_n\to g$ uniformly on $E$; (2) $f,g$ are bounded on $E$ — then $f_ng_n\to fg$ uniformly on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Cesàro Mean:} If $b_k\to b$, then $\frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}\to b$. Equivalently, Stolz-Cesàro: if $c_n\to c$ and $a_n$ monotone or $d_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\to\infty$, then $\lim\frac{a_n}{d_n}=L\implies\lim\frac{\sum a_k}{\sum d_k}=L$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Arith. Mean Conv:} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ bounded $\implies$ $\frac{f_1+\dots+f_n}{n}\to f$ uniformly on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Differentiability (7.12):} (1) $(a,b)$ bounded; (2) each $f_n$ diff on $(a,b)$; (3) $f_n(x_0)\to L$ for some $x_0$; (4) $f_n'$ converges uniformly on $(a,b)$ $\implies$ $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $(a,b)$ and $f'=\lim f_n'$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform Cauchy Criterion (7.11):} $f_n$ conv uniformly on $E$ $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n,m\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Weierstrass M-Test (7.15):} $|f_k(x)|\le M_k$ for $x\in E$, $\sum M_k<\infty\implies\sum f_k$ abs conv and uniformly on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Term-by-Term Diff (7.14):} (1) $I$ open interval; (2) each $f_k$ differentiable on $I$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges at some $x_0\in I$; (4) $\sum f_k'$ converges uniformly on $I$ $\implies$ $(\sum f_k)'=\sum f_k'$ on $I$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Term-by-Term Int (7.14):} (1) $[a,b]$ closed; (2) each $f_k$ integrable on $[a,b]$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges uniformly on $[a,b]$ $\implies$ $\int_a^b\sum f_k=\sum\int_a^b f_k$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Term-by-Term Cont (7.14):} (1) $E$ set; (2) each $f_k$ continuous on $E$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges uniformly on $E$ $\implies$ $\sum f_k$ continuous on $E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test for Uniform Conv (7.16):} $|\sum_{k=1}^n f_k(x)|\le M$ for all $n,x\in E$ and $g_k\downarrow0$ uniformly $\implies\sum f_kg_k$ converges uniformly.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Power Series Radius (7.21):} $S(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$, $R=1/\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $S$ abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, uniformly on any $[a,b]\subset(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{PS Diff \& Int (7.26,7.32):} On $(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, $S\in C^\infty$ and $S'(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty k a_k(x-x_0)^{k-1}$, $\int S=\sum\frac{a_k}{k+1}(x-x_0)^{k+1}+C$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Abel's Theorem (7.27):} If $\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ converges on $[a,b]$, then it converges uniformly on $[a,b]$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniqueness (7.39):} If $f(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ on open interval $I$, then $a_k=f^{(k)}(x_0)/k!$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$: ptwise $f_n\to0$ for $x<1$, $f_n(1)=1$, so not continuous at $x=1$ (non-uniform). $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,r]$, $r<1$: uniform conv (M-test: $M_k=r^k$, $\sum r^k<\infty$). $f_n(x)=x^n(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$: uniform conv by M-test ($x^n(1-x)\le 1$).

\section*{Ch8. Euclidean Spaces $\mathbb R^n$}

\textbf{Topological Definitions:}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item Open ball: $B_r(a)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x-a\|<r\}$. Closed ball: $\{\|x-a\|\le r\}$.
\item $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ is \textbf{open}: $\forall a\in V$, $\exists\varepsilon>0:B_\varepsilon(a)\subset V$.
\item $E$ is \textbf{closed}: $E^c$ is open.
\item \textbf{Relatively open in }$A$: $E\subset A$ is relatively open if $E=A\cap V$ for some open $V$.
\item \textbf{Relatively closed in }$A$: $E=A\cap F$ for some closed $F$.
\item \textbf{Compact}: every open cover has a finite subcover.
\item \textbf{Connected}: cannot be separated into two nonempty disjoint relatively-open sets.
\item \textbf{Interior} $E^\circ$: union of all open subsets of $E$ (largest open set $\subset E$).
\item \textbf{Closure} $\overline{E}$: intersection of all closed supersets of $E$ (smallest closed set $\supset E$).
\item \textbf{Boundary} $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$.
\item \textbf{Limit point/accumulation point}: $x$ is limit point of $E$ if every $B_\varepsilon(x)$ contains $y\in E$ with $y\ne x$.
\item $E$ is \textbf{perfect}: $E$ is closed and every point of $E$ is a limit point of $E$.
\item \textbf{Dense}: $\overline{E}=\mathbb R^n$ (or $\overline{E}\cap U\neq\varnothing$ for every open $U$).
\item \textbf{Sequentially compact}: every sequence has a convergent subsequence.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} $\mathbb Q$ is dense in $\mathbb R$. $(0,1)$ is open, not closed. $[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q$ is not closed, not open. $\mathbb R^n$ is connected. $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ is connected. Cantor set is perfect and nowhere dense.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Cauchy-Schwarz (8.5):} $|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, equality $\iff x,y$ parallel or one is zero.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Triangle Inequalities (8.6):} $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$, $\|x-y\|\ge|\|x\|-\|y\||$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Norm Inequalities (8.7):} $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$, $\|x\|\le\|x\|_1\le\sqrt n\|x\|$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Heine-Borel (9.11):} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ compact $\iff$ $E$ is closed and bounded.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Closed $\iff$ Sequential (9.8):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $x_k\in E$, $x_k\to x$ $\implies x\in E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Limit Point Char (9.7):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $E$ contains all its limit points.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Open/Closed Properties (8.24):} Arbitrary unions of open are open; finite intersections of open are open. Arbitrary intersections of closed are closed; finite unions of closed are closed.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Connected $\iff$ Interval (8.30):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ connected $\iff$ $E$ is an interval. Rectangles in $\mathbb R^n$ are connected.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Linear Maps (8.15-8.18):} $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ linear $\iff$ $T(x)=Bx$ for unique $m\times n$ matrix $B$. Operator norm: $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\neq0}\frac{\|T(x)\|}{\|x\|}$, and $\|T(x)\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Distance Between Sets (8.33):} $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{\|x-y\|:x\in A,y\in B\}$. If $A,B$ are compact and disjoint, then $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Cross Product (8.9):} $x,y\in\mathbb R^3$: $x\times y\perp x$ and $x\times y\perp y$. $\|x\times y\|=\|x\|\|y\|\sin\theta$. $x\times(y\times z)=(x\cdot z)y-(x\cdot y)z$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Balls are Open/Closed (8.21):} Open ball $B_r(a)$ is open; closed ball $\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is closed. Shell $\{x:s\le\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is neither open nor closed.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Relatively Open/Closed of Subset (8.26):} If $C\subset E\subset\mathbb R^n$: (1) $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ relatively open in $E$. (2) $C$ relatively open in $E$ + $E$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Closure/Interior Monotonicity (8.34):} $A\subset B$ $\implies$ $\overline{A}\subset\overline{B}$ and $A^\circ\subset B^\circ$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Interior/Closure of Subsets:} If $U\subset E$ relatively open in $E$: (1) If $U\subset E^\circ$, then $U\cap\partial E=\varnothing$. (2) If $U\cap\partial E\neq\varnothing$, then $U\cap\partial U=U\cap\partial E$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{$\overline{A\cap B}\neq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$ in general. $(A\cup B)^\circ\neq A^\circ\cup B^\circ$ in general.}

\section*{Ch9. Convergence in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\dots,x_k^{(n)})\to a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\iff x_k^{(j)}\to a_j$ for each $j$.
\item Bounded: $\exists M>0:\|x_k\|\le M\ \forall k$.
\item Cauchy: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:k,m\ge N\implies\|x_k-x_m\|<\varepsilon$.
\item $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to a$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists\delta>0:0<\|x-a\|<\delta\implies\|f(x)-L\|<\varepsilon$.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\textbf{Conv $\iff$ Componentwise (9.2):} $x_k^{(j)}\to a_j\ \forall j\iff x_k\to a$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Sequence Properties (9.4,9.6):} Uniqueness. Subseq $\to$ same limit. Conv $\implies$ bounded. Conv $\iff$ Cauchy.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Bolzano-Weierstrass (9.5):} Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb R^n$ has a convergent subsequence.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Limit Laws (9.15):} $\lim(f+g)=L+M$, $\lim(\alpha f)=\alpha L$, $\lim(f\cdot g)=L\cdot M$. Squeeze: $g\le h\le f$, $\lim f=\lim g=L\implies\lim h=L$. Composition: $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L$, $\lim_{y\to L}h(y)=M\implies\lim_{x\to a}h(g(x))=M$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Limit $\iff$ Sequential (9.15ii):} $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\iff f(x_k)\to L$ for every $x_k\to a$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuous $\iff$ Preimage of Open (9.26):} $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\iff$ $f^{-1}(V)$ relatively open in $E$ for every open $V\subset\mathbb R^m$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Compact $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (9.29):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous on $K$ $\implies f(K)$ compact. Hence $f$ bounded and attains max/min (Extreme Value Thm 9.32).\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity $\Rightarrow$ Connectedness (9.30):} $E$ connected, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f(E)$ is connected.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuous Inverse (9.33):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ is 1-1 and continuous $\implies f^{-1}$ continuous on $f(K)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Uniform Continuity on Compact (9.25):} $E$ compact, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f$ uniformly continuous.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Dini's Theorem (9.40):} $K$ compact, $f_k:K\to\mathbb R$ ptwise monotone to continuous $f$ $\implies f_k\to f$ uniformly on $K$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Continuity $\iff$ Coord-wise (9.18):} $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m):E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous at $a$ $\iff$ each $f_j$ is continuous at $a$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Dot Product Conv (9.22):} $x_k\to0$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $y_k$ bounded in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $x_k\cdot y_k\to0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Compact + Isolated Points $\implies$ Finite (9.12):} $K$ compact, each $x\in K$ isolated ($\exists r>0:B_r(x)\cap K=\{x\}$) $\implies$ $K$ is finite.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} $f(x,y)=x^2+xy$, $g(x,y)=\sin(xy)$. To check $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f(x,y)=0$: use $|x^2+xy|\le|x|^2+|x||y|\le|x|^2+|x||y|$. With $|y|\le r$, $\le r^2+er^2\to0$. For $f(x)=1/(x_1^2+\dots+x_n^2)$: no limit as $x\to0$ (unbounded), not continuous at $0$.

\section*{Ch10. Differentiation in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $f:V\to\mathbb R^m$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open. $f$ diff at $a\in V$ $\iff$ $\exists$ linear $Df(a):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ s.t. $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Df(a)h\|}{\|h\|}=0$.
\item $Df(a)$ = Jacobian. If $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$, then $Df=(J_{ij})$, $J_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

Continuity $\not\Rightarrow$ Differentiability. $f$ diff at $a$ $\implies$ all partials exist and $f$ continuous.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} $f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$, $f(0,0)=0$. Partial derivatives at $(0,0)$: $f_x(0,0)=0$, $f_y(0,0)=0$, but $f$ is not differentiable at $(0,0)$ because $\|f(h)-0-Df(0)h\|/\|h\|=1/2\not\to0$ along $y=x$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Chain Rule (10.3):} $D(f\circ g)(a)=Df(g(a))Dg(a)$. Scalar: $\partial f/\partial x_i=\sum_j\frac{\partial f}{\partial u_j}\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Equality of Mixed Partials (10.6):} If: (1) $f_{xy}$ exists in a neighborhood of $(a,b)$; (2) $f_{yx}$ exists at $(a,b)$; (3) $f_{yx}$ is continuous at $(a,b)$ — then $f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b)$. In particular, if $f\in C^2$, then $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Euler's Homogeneous Function Thm (10.9):} $f\in C^1$, homogeneous of degree $k$ ($f(tx)=t^kf(x)$) $\implies x\cdot\nabla f(x)=k f(x)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Mean Value Theorem (Inequality) (10.12):} If: (1) $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ open and connected; (2) $f:U\to\mathbb R$ differentiable; (3) $\|Df(x)\|\le M$ for all $x\in U$ — then $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in U$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Taylor's Theorem (10.14):} $f\in C^{k+1}$: $f(b)=f(a)+\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{j!}(D^jf(a))(b-a)^j+\frac1{(k+1)!}(D^{k+1}f(c))(b-a)^{k+1}$ for some $c$ on $[a,b]$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Taylor 2nd Order, 2 vars (10.16):} $f(a+h,b+k)=f(a,b)+hf_x+kf_y+\frac12(h^2f_{xx}+2hkf_{xy}+k^2f_{yy})+o(h^2+k^2)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Inverse Function Theorem (11.6):} Let $f:V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, $f\in C^1$, $a\in V$, $Df(a)$ invertible. Then: (1) $\exists$ open $U\ni a$, $W\ni f(a)$ s.t. $f|_U$ is 1-1 and $f(U)=W$; (2) $f^{-1}\in C^1$ on $W$; (3) $Df^{-1}(f(x))=[Df(x)]^{-1}$ $\forall x\in U$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex (Inverse FT):} $f(x)=x^3+x-1$, $f'(x)=3x^2+1>0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing, $C^1$, $Df(x)\neq0$. $f(0)=-1$, $f(1)=1$, so by continuity $\exists$ unique $C^1$ inverse on $[f(0),f(1)]$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Implicit Function Theorem (11.47):} Let $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}$ open, $F\in C^1$, $F(a,b)=0$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$. If $\det\frac{\partial(F_1,\dots,F_n)}{\partial(x_1,\dots,x_n)}(a,b)\neq0$, then: (1) $\exists$ open $W\subset\mathbb R^p$ with $b\in W$; (2) $\exists$ unique $C^1$ function $g:W\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(b)=a$ and $F(g(t),t)=0$ $\forall t\in W$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex (Implicit FT):} $F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1$. $F(a,b)=0$, $\partial F/\partial x=2x$. At $(a,b)=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$, $\partial F/\partial x\neq0$, so locally $y=g(x)$ solves $x^2+g(x)^2=1$. Indeed $g(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ near this point.

\section*{Ch11. Integration in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:} $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ bounded.
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item Darboux sums: $U(P,f)=\sum M_i\Delta x_i$, $L(P,f)=\sum m_i\Delta x_i$.
\item $f\in\mathcal R$ (Riemann integrable) $\iff\sup_P L(P,f)=\inf_P U(P,f)$.
\item Equivalent: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists P$ s.t. $U(P,f)-L(P,f)<\varepsilon$.
\item $f$ continuous a.e.: discontinuities have measure zero.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} Dirichlet's function $f(x)=1$ if $x\in\mathbb Q$, $0$ if $x\notin\mathbb Q$ on $[0,1]$: every point is a discontinuity, so not Riemann integrable. Thomae's function $f(x)=1/q$ if $x=p/q$ in lowest terms, $0$ if irrational: continuous at all irrationals (measure 0 discontinuities), so Riemann integrable with $\int_0^1 f=0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Lebesgue's Theorem (9.49):} Bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Elementary Integrability:} Every monotone function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable. Every step function is integrable. If $f\in\mathcal R$ and $g=f$ a.e., then $g\in\mathcal R$ and $\int g=\int f$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Integral Properties:} If $f,g\in\mathcal R[a,b]$, then $f+g$, $cf$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, and $fg$ are all in $\mathcal R$. Also $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{FTC (4.4,5.3):}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $F\in C^1[a,b]$, $F'=f$ a.e., $f\in\mathcal R$ $\implies$ $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$.
\item $f\in\mathcal R[a,b]$, $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ $\implies$ $F$ continuous and $F'(x)=f(x)$ a.e.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\textbf{MVT for Integrals (5.8):} $f\in\mathcal R[a,b]$, $m\le f\le M$ $\implies\exists c\in[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f=(b-a)f(c)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Differentiating Under Integral (11.4):} $f(x,y)$ continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$ $\implies$
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $F(y)=\int_a^b f(x,y)dx$ continuous on $[c,d]$.
\item If $f_y$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$, then $F'(y)=\int_a^b f_y(x,y)dx$.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\section*{Ch12. Lebesgue Measure}
\textbf{Outer Measure $m^*$:} For $E\subset\mathbb R$, $m^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum|I_j|:\cup I_j\supset E,\ \{I_j\}\text{ countable open intervals}\right\}$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Measurable (Carathéodory, 7.2):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ is Lebesgue measurable $\iff$ $m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ $\forall A\subset\mathbb R$. Equivalently: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ open $U\supset E$ with $m^*(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Lebesgue Measure $m$:} $m(E)=m^*(E)$ for all measurable $E$. All open sets, closed sets, intervals, Borel sets are measurable. $\mathbb Q$, countable sets, null sets are measurable with $m(E)=0$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Defs (Functions/Integral):}
\begin{itemize}[left=0pt, itemsep=0pt, topsep=0pt, parsep=0pt]
\item $E\subset\mathbb R$ has measure zero ($m(E)=0$): $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ countable cover $\{I_j\}$ with $\sum|I_j|<\varepsilon$.
\item Almost everywhere (a.e.): property holds a.e. if the set where it fails has measure zero.
\item $f$ Lebesgue measurable: $\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $\{f>\alpha\}$ is measurable (equivalently $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$).
\item Lebesgue integral: $\int_E f=\sup\{\int_E\phi:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ simple}\}$.
\item $f\in L^1$: $|f|$ integrable ($\int|f|<\infty$). For $f$ possibly signed: $\int f=\int f^+-\int f^-$, defined when $\int|f|<\infty$.
\end{itemize}\\[2pt]

\textbf{Ex:} $f_n=\mathbf1_{[n,n+1]}$, $\int f_n=1$ but $f_n\to0$ ptwise. Lebesgue integral still $0$. $\sum f_n=\infty$ on $[0,\infty)$ but finite a.e. at each point — MCT gives $\int\sum f_n=\sum\int f_n=\infty$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Ex (DCT):} $f_n=n\mathbf1_{[0,1/n]}$: $f_n\to0$ a.e., $|f_n|\le g$ with $g\equiv1\in L^1$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0$. (Riemann: $f_n$ not integrable for any $n$ if treated as a function on $[0,1]$ with varying domain.)\\l

\textbf{Null Sets (7.2):} Every countable set has measure zero. Finite/countable union of null sets is null. $m(E)=0\implies E$ is measurable.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Properties of Measurable Sets (7.3):} $\sigma$-algebra: $E$ meas. $\implies$ $E^c$ meas.; countable unions $\cup E_k$, countable intersections $\cap E_k$ of meas. sets are meas. (hence all Borel sets are meas.). $m(\varnothing)=0$, $m((a,b))=b-a$. Finite additivity: $E\cap F=\varnothing$ $\implies$ $m(E\cup F)=m(E)+m(F)$. Countable additivity: $\{E_k\}$ disjoint $\implies$ $m(\cup E_k)=\sum m(E_k)$. Continuity from below/above: $E_k\uparrow E$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\uparrow m(E)$; $E_k\downarrow E$, $m(E_1)<\infty$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\downarrow m(E)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties (7.1):} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli Lemma (7.5):} $\sum m(\Omega_k)<\infty$ $\implies$ $x\in\Omega_k$ for infinitely many $k$ has measure zero (i.e., a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $\Omega_k$).\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Monotone Convergence (MCT, 11.23):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable, $f_k\uparrow f$ a.e. $\implies\int f_k\uparrow\int f$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Dominated Convergence (DCT, 11.30):} If: (1) $f_k\to f$ a.e.; (2) $|f_k|\le g$ for all $k$ a.e.; (3) $g\in L^1$ ($\int|g|<\infty$) — then $\int f_k\to\int f$ and $f\in L^1$. (Most commonly used.)\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Fatou's Lemma (11.25):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable $\implies\int\liminf f_k\le\liminf\int f_k$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Riemann $\iff$ Lebesgue + Measure Zero (9.49):} For bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$: $f$ Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e., and the two integrals agree.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{$L^p$ Spaces (11.43):} $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. H\"older: $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Minkowski: $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral Properties (11.33):} Let $f,g\in L^1(\Omega)$. Then: (1) linearity: $\int(cf+g)=c\int f+\int g$ for any $c\in\mathbb R$; (2) if $f\le g$ a.e. then $\int f\le\int g$; (3) if $f=g$ a.e. then $\int f=\int g$; (4) $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Integral (11.34):} $f_k\in L^1$, $f_k\to f$ a.e., $|f_k|\le g$ with $g\in L^1$ $\implies$ $f\in L^1$ and $\int f_k\to\int f$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e. (11.35):} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e. (set $\{f=\infty\}$ has measure zero).\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity/Measurability of Composite (11.18):} $f$ measurable, $g$ continuous $\implies$ $g\circ f$ measurable. $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ measurable $\iff$ each $f_j$ measurable. $f$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ measurable $\forall a$.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Almost everywhere modification (11.19):} $f$ Lebesgue measurable, $g=f$ a.e. $\implies$ $g$ is Lebesgue measurable.\\[-2pt]

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Measurable Functions (11.18):} $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ measurable, $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$.\\[-2pt]

\end{multicols}

\documentclass[8pt]{extarticle}
\usepackage[margin=0.15in, landscape, top=0.12in, bottom=0.12in, left=0.12in, right=0.12in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath, amssymb, enumitem}
\usepackage{mathtools}
\usepackage{parskip}
\usepackage{multicol}

\begin{document}
\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\fontsize{6pt}{7.5pt}\selectfont
\addtolength{\baselineskip}{-1.5pt}
\addtolength{\columnsep}{-2pt}
\setlength{\itemsep}{-3pt}
\setlength{\topsep}{-2pt}
\setlength{\partopsep}{0pt}
\setlength{\parsep}{-1pt}

\begin{multicols}{3}

\section*{Ch6. Infinite Series of Real Numbers}
\textbf{Defs:} $s_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k$. $\sum a_k$ converges to $s$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|s_n-s|<\varepsilon$. Diverges: $\{s_n\}$ has no limit. Abs conv: $\sum|a_k|<\infty$. Conditional: conv but not abs.\smallskip

\textbf{Divergence Test (6.5):} $a_k\not\to0\implies\sum a_k$ diverges.\smallskip

\textbf{Geometric (6.7):} $\sum_{k=0}^\infty x^k=\frac1{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$, diverges for $|x|\ge1$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cauchy Criterion (6.8):} $\sum a_k$ conv $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:m\ge n\ge N\implies\sum_{k=n}^m a_k<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Comparison (6.14):} $0\le a_k\le b_k$ for large $k$: $\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$; $\sum a_k=\infty\implies\sum b_k=\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{LCT (6.16):} $L=\lim a_k/b_k$, $b_k>0$. $0<L<\infty$: same conv. $L=0$+$\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$. $L=\infty$+$\sum b_k=\infty\implies\sum a_k=\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Test (6.12):} $f\ge0$ decr on $[1,\infty)$. $\sum f(k)$ conv $\iff\int_1^\infty f<\infty$. $\sum1/k^p$ conv $\iff p>1$.\smallskip

\textbf{Root Test (6.23):} $r=\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Ratio Test (6.24):} $r=\lim|a_{k+1}/a_k|$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $\sum k/e^k$ conv by ratio test ($r=1/e<1$). $\sum k^2/(k+1)$ diverges ($a_k\to\infty$). $\sum1/k^2$ conv ($p=2>1$). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond conv ($|a_k|=1/k$, abs diverges).\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Conv (6.20):} Abs conv $\implies$conv (converse false). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Rearrangements (6.27):} If $\sum a_k$ abs conv, every rearrangement $\to$ same sum. Cond conv $\implies$ can rearrange to any $x\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abel's Formula (6.30):} $A_{n,m}=\sum_{k=m}^n a_k$. $\sum_{k=m}^n a_kb_k=A_{n,m}b_n-\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}A_{k,m}(b_{k+1}-b_k)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test (6.31):} $\sum a_k$ partial sums bounded + $b_k\downarrow0$ $\implies\sum a_kb_k$ converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Alt Series Test (6.32):} $a_k\downarrow0\implies\sum(-1)^ka_k$ converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Alt Series Error (6.38):} $a_k\downarrow0$, $s=\sum(-1)^ka_k$, $|s-s_n|\le a_{n+1}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Test Error (6.35):} $0\le\sum_{k=1}^n f(k)-\int_1^n f\le f(1)$. If $\sum f(k)$ conv: $0\le s-s_n+\int_n^\infty f\le f(n)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Logarithmic Test (6.42):} $p=\lim\frac{\log(1/|a_k|)}{\log k}$. $p>1\implies$abs conv; $p<1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Raabe's Test (6.43):} $|a_{k+1}/a_k|\le1-p/k+O(1/k)$ with $p>1\implies\sum a_k$ abs conv.\smallskip

\section*{Ch7. Infinite Series of Functions}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f_n\to f$ ptwise: $\forall x\in E$, $\lim f_n(x)=f(x)$. $f_n\to f$ uniformly: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$ ($N$ depends only on $\varepsilon$). Radius of conv $R$: abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (7.9):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ cont at $x_0\in E$ $\implies f$ cont at $x_0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Integrability (7.10):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$, each integrable $\implies f$ integrable and $\int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Boundedness + Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} $f_n$ uniformly bounded on $E$ ($\exists M:|f_n(x)|\le M$ $\forall n,x$) + $f_n\to f$ uniformly $\implies f$ bounded on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$ and each $f_n$ bounded on $E$, then $f$ is bounded on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Product of Uniformly Conv Functions:} If: (1) $f_n\to f$, $g_n\to g$ uniformly on $E$; (2) $f,g$ bounded on $E$ — then $f_ng_n\to fg$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cesàro Mean:} If $b_k\to b$, then $\frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}\to b$. Equivalently, Stolz-Cesàro: if $c_n\to c$ and $a_n$ monotone or $d_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\to\infty$, then $\lim\frac{a_n}{d_n}=L\implies\lim\frac{\sum a_k}{\sum d_k}=L$.\smallskip

\textbf{Arith. Mean Conv:} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ bounded $\implies$ $\frac{f_1+\dots+f_n}{n}\to f$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Differentiability (7.12):} (1) $(a,b)$ bounded; (2) each $f_n$ diff on $(a,b)$; (3) $f_n(x_0)\to L$ for some $x_0$; (4) $f_n'$ converges uniformly on $(a,b)$ $\implies$ $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $(a,b)$ and $f'=\lim f_n'$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Cauchy Criterion (7.11):} $f_n$ conv uniformly on $E$ $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n,m\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Weierstrass M-Test (7.15):} $|f_k(x)|\le M_k$ for $x\in E$, $\sum M_k<\infty\implies\sum f_k$ abs conv and uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Diff (7.14):} (1) $I$ open interval; (2) each $f_k$ differentiable on $I$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges at some $x_0\in I$; (4) $\sum f_k'$ converges uniformly on $I$ $\implies$ $(\sum f_k)'=\sum f_k'$ on $I$.\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Int (7.14):} (1) $[a,b]$ closed; (2) each $f_k$ integrable on $[a,b]$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges uniformly on $[a,b]$ $\implies$ $\int_a^b\sum f_k=\sum\int_a^b f_k$.\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Cont (7.14):} (1) $E$ set; (2) each $f_k$ continuous on $E$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges uniformly on $E$ $\implies$ $\sum f_k$ continuous on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test for Uniform Conv (7.16):} $|\sum_{k=1}^n f_k(x)|\le M$ for all $n,x\in E$ and $g_k\downarrow0$ uniformly $\implies\sum f_kg_k$ converges uniformly.\smallskip

\textbf{Power Series Radius (7.21):} $S(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$, $R=1/\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $S$ abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, uniformly on any $[a,b]\subset(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.\smallskip

\textbf{PS Diff \& Int (7.26,7.32):} On $(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, $S\in C^\infty$ and $S'(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty k a_k(x-x_0)^{k-1}$, $\int S=\sum\frac{a_k}{k+1}(x-x_0)^{k+1}+C$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abel's Theorem (7.27):} If $\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ converges on $[a,b]$, then it converges uniformly on $[a,b]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniqueness (7.39):} If $f(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ on open interval $I$, then $a_k=f^{(k)}(x_0)/k!$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$: ptwise $f_n\to0$ for $x<1$, $f_n(1)=1$, so not continuous at $x=1$ (non-uniform). $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,r]$, $r<1$: uniform conv (M-test: $M_k=r^k$, $\sum r^k<\infty$). $f_n(x)=x^n(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$: uniform conv by M-test ($x^n(1-x)\le 1$).\smallskip

\section*{Ch8. Euclidean Spaces $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Topological Definitions:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent Open ball: $B_r(a)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x-a\|<r\}$. Closed ball: $\{\|x-a\|\le r\}$. $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ is \textbf{open}: $\forall a\in V$, $\exists\varepsilon>0:B_\varepsilon(a)\subset V$. $E$ is \textbf{closed}: $E^c$ is open. \textbf{Relatively open in} $A$: $E\subset A$ is relatively open if $E=A\cap V$ for some open $V$. \textbf{Relatively closed in} $A$: $E=A\cap F$ for some closed $F$. \textbf{Compact}: every open cover has a finite subcover. \textbf{Connected}: cannot be separated into two nonempty disjoint relatively-open sets. \textbf{Interior} $E^\circ$: union of all open subsets of $E$ (largest open set $\subset E$). \textbf{Closure} $\overline{E}$: intersection of all closed supersets of $E$ (smallest closed set $\supset E$). \textbf{Boundary} $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$. \textbf{Limit point}: $x$ is limit point of $E$ if every $B_\varepsilon(x)$ contains $y\in E$ with $y\ne x$. $E$ is \textbf{perfect}: $E$ is closed and every point of $E$ is a limit point of $E$. \textbf{Dense}: $\overline{E}=\mathbb R^n$ (or $\overline{E}\cap U\neq\varnothing$ for every open $U$). \textbf{Sequentially compact}: every sequence has a convergent subsequence.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $\mathbb Q$ is dense in $\mathbb R$. $(0,1)$ is open, not closed. $[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q$ is not closed, not open. $\mathbb R^n$ is connected. $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ is connected. Cantor set is perfect and nowhere dense.\smallskip

\textbf{Cauchy-Schwarz (8.5):} $|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, equality $\iff x,y$ parallel or one is zero.\smallskip

\textbf{Triangle Inequalities (8.6):} $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$, $\|x-y\|\ge|\|x\|-\|y\||$.\smallskip

\textbf{Norm Inequalities (8.7):} $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$, $\|x\|\le\|x\|_1\le\sqrt n\|x\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Heine-Borel (9.11):} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ compact $\iff$ $E$ is closed and bounded.\smallskip

\textbf{Closed $\iff$ Sequential (9.8):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $x_k\in E$, $x_k\to x$ $\implies x\in E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit Point Char (9.7):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $E$ contains all its limit points.\smallskip

\textbf{Open/Closed Properties (8.24):} Arbitrary unions of open are open; finite intersections of open are open. Arbitrary intersections of closed are closed; finite unions of closed are closed.\smallskip

\textbf{Connected $\iff$ Interval (8.30):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ connected $\iff$ $E$ is an interval. Rectangles in $\mathbb R^n$ are connected.\smallskip

\textbf{Linear Maps (8.15-8.18):} $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ linear $\iff$ $T(x)=Bx$ for unique $m\times n$ matrix $B$. Operator norm: $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\neq0}\frac{\|T(x)\|}{\|x\|}$, and $\|T(x)\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Distance Between Sets (8.33):} $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{\|x-y\|:x\in A,y\in B\}$. If $A,B$ are compact and disjoint, then $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cross Product (8.9):} $x,y\in\mathbb R^3$: $x\times y\perp x$ and $x\times y\perp y$. $\|x\times y\|=\|x\|\|y\|\sin\theta$. $x\times(y\times z)=(x\cdot z)y-(x\cdot y)z$.\smallskip

\textbf{Balls are Open/Closed (8.21):} Open ball $B_r(a)$ is open; closed ball $\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is closed. Shell $\{x:s\le\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is neither open nor closed.\smallskip

\textbf{Relatively Open/Closed of Subset (8.26):} If $C\subset E\subset\mathbb R^n$: (1) $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ relatively open in $E$. (2) $C$ relatively open in $E$ + $E$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$.\smallskip

\textbf{Closure/Interior Monotonicity (8.34):} $A\subset B$ $\implies$ $\overline{A}\subset\overline{B}$ and $A^\circ\subset B^\circ$.\smallskip

\textbf{Interior/Closure of Subsets:} If $U\subset E$ relatively open in $E$: (1) If $U\subset E^\circ$, then $U\cap\partial E=\varnothing$. (2) If $U\cap\partial E\neq\varnothing$, then $U\cap\partial U=U\cap\partial E$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\overline{A\cap B}\neq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$ in general. $(A\cup B)^\circ\neq A^\circ\cup B^\circ$ in general.}\smallskip

\section*{Ch9. Convergence in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\dots,x_k^{(n)})\to a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\iff x_k^{(j)}\to a_j$ for each $j$. Bounded: $\exists M>0:\|x_k\|\le M\ \forall k$. Cauchy: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:k,m\ge N\implies\|x_k-x_m\|<\varepsilon$. $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to a$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists\delta>0:0<\|x-a\|<\delta\implies\|f(x)-L\|<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Conv $\iff$ Componentwise (9.2):} $x_k^{(j)}\to a_j\ \forall j\iff x_k\to a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Sequence Properties (9.4,9.6):} Uniqueness. Subseq $\to$ same limit. Conv $\implies$ bounded. Conv $\iff$ Cauchy.\smallskip

\textbf{Bolzano-Weierstrass (9.5):} Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb R^n$ has a convergent subsequence.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit Laws (9.15):} $\lim(f+g)=L+M$, $\lim(\alpha f)=\alpha L$, $\lim(f\cdot g)=L\cdot M$. Squeeze: $g\le h\le f$, $\lim f=\lim g=L\implies\lim h=L$. Composition: $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L$, $\lim_{y\to L}h(y)=M\implies\lim_{x\to a}h(g(x))=M$.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit $\iff$ Sequential (9.15ii):} $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\iff f(x_k)\to L$ for every $x_k\to a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous $\iff$ Preimage of Open (9.26):} $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\iff$ $f^{-1}(V)$ relatively open in $E$ for every open $V\subset\mathbb R^m$.\smallskip

\textbf{Compact $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (9.29):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous on $K$ $\implies f(K)$ compact. Hence $f$ bounded and attains max/min (Extreme Value Thm 9.32).\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity $\Rightarrow$ Connectedness (9.30):} $E$ connected, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f(E)$ is connected.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous Inverse (9.33):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ is 1-1 and continuous $\implies f^{-1}$ continuous on $f(K)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Continuity on Compact (9.25):} $E$ compact, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f$ uniformly continuous.\smallskip

\textbf{Dini's Theorem (9.40):} $K$ compact, $f_k:K\to\mathbb R$ ptwise monotone to continuous $f$ $\implies f_k\to f$ uniformly on $K$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Continuity $\iff$ Coord-wise (9.18):} $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m):E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous at $a$ $\iff$ each $f_j$ is continuous at $a$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Dot Product Conv (9.22):} $x_k\to0$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $y_k$ bounded in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $x_k\cdot y_k\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Compact + Isolated Points $\implies$ Finite (9.12):} $K$ compact, each $x\in K$ isolated ($\exists r>0:B_r(x)\cap K=\{x\}$) $\implies$ $K$ is finite.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $f(x,y)=x^2+xy$, $g(x,y)=\sin(xy)$. To check $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f(x,y)=0$: use $|x^2+xy|\le|x|^2+|x||y|$. With $|y|\le r$, $\le r^2+er^2\to0$. For $f(x)=1/(x_1^2+\dots+x_n^2)$: no limit as $x\to0$ (unbounded), not continuous at $0$.\smallskip

\section*{Ch10. Differentiation in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f:V\to\mathbb R^m$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open. $f$ diff at $a\in V$ $\iff$ $\exists$ linear $Df(a):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ s.t. $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Df(a)h\|}{\|h\|}=0$. $Df(a)$ = Jacobian. If $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$, then $Df=(J_{ij})$, $J_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$.\smallskip

Continuity $\not\Rightarrow$ Differentiability. $f$ diff at $a$ $\implies$ all partials exist and $f$ continuous.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$, $f(0,0)=0$. Partial derivatives at $(0,0)$: $f_x(0,0)=0$, $f_y(0,0)=0$, but $f$ is not differentiable at $(0,0)$ because $\|f(h)-0-Df(0)h\|/\|h\|=1/2\not\to0$ along $y=x$.\smallskip

\textbf{Chain Rule (10.3):} $D(f\circ g)(a)=Df(g(a))Dg(a)$. Scalar: $\partial f/\partial x_i=\sum_j\frac{\partial f}{\partial u_j}\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Equality of Mixed Partials (10.6):} If: (1) $f_{xy}$ exists in a neighborhood of $(a,b)$; (2) $f_{yx}$ exists at $(a,b)$; (3) $f_{yx}$ is continuous at $(a,b)$ — then $f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b)$. In particular, if $f\in C^2$, then $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Euler's Homogeneous Function Thm (10.9):} $f\in C^1$, homogeneous of degree $k$ ($f(tx)=t^kf(x)$) $\implies x\cdot\nabla f(x)=k f(x)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Mean Value Theorem (Inequality) (10.12):} If: (1) $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ open and connected; (2) $f:U\to\mathbb R$ differentiable; (3) $\|Df(x)\|\le M$ for all $x\in U$ — then $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in U$.\smallskip

\textbf{Taylor's Theorem (10.14):} $f\in C^{k+1}$: $f(b)=f(a)+\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{j!}(D^jf(a))(b-a)^j+\frac1{(k+1)!}(D^{k+1}f(c))(b-a)^{k+1}$ for some $c$ on $[a,b]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Taylor 2nd Order, 2 vars (10.16):} $f(a+h,b+k)=f(a,b)+hf_x+kf_y+\frac12(h^2f_{xx}+2hkf_{xy}+k^2f_{yy})+o(h^2+k^2)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Inverse Function Theorem (11.6):} Let $f:V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, $f\in C^1$, $a\in V$, $Df(a)$ invertible. Then: (1) $\exists$ open $U\ni a$, $W\ni f(a)$ s.t. $f|_U$ is 1-1 and $f(U)=W$; (2) $f^{-1}\in C^1$ on $W$; (3) $Df^{-1}(f(x))=[Df(x)]^{-1}$ $\forall x\in U$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Inverse FT):} $f(x)=x^3+x-1$, $f'(x)=3x^2+1>0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing, $C^1$, $Df(x)\neq0$. $f(0)=-1$, $f(1)=1$, so by continuity $\exists$ unique $C^1$ inverse on $[f(0),f(1)]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Implicit Function Theorem (11.47):} Let $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}$ open, $F\in C^1$, $F(a,b)=0$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$. If $\det\frac{\partial(F_1,\dots,F_n)}{\partial(x_1,\dots,x_n)}(a,b)\neq0$, then: (1) $\exists$ open $W\subset\mathbb R^p$ with $b\in W$; (2) $\exists$ unique $C^1$ function $g:W\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(b)=a$ and $F(g(t),t)=0$ $\forall t\in W$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Implicit FT):} $F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1$. $F(a,b)=0$, $\partial F/\partial x=2x$. At $(a,b)=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$, $\partial F/\partial x\neq0$, so locally $y=g(x)$ solves $x^2+g(x)^2=1$. Indeed $g(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ near this point.\smallskip

\section*{Ch11. Integration in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ bounded. Darboux sums: $U(P,f)=\sum M_i\Delta x_i$, $L(P,f)=\sum m_i\Delta x_i$. $f\in\mathcal R$ (Riemann integrable) $\iff\sup_P L(P,f)=\inf_P U(P,f)$. Equivalent: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists P$ s.t. $U(P,f)-L(P,f)<\varepsilon$. $f$ continuous a.e.: discontinuities have measure zero.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} Dirichlet's function $f(x)=1$ if $x\in\mathbb Q$, $0$ if $x\notin\mathbb Q$ on $[0,1]$: every point is a discontinuity, so not Riemann integrable. Thomae's function $f(x)=1/q$ if $x=p/q$ in lowest terms, $0$ if irrational: continuous at all irrationals (measure 0 discontinuities), so Riemann integrable with $\int_0^1 f=0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue's Theorem (9.49):} Bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e.\smallskip

\textbf{Elementary Integrability:} Every monotone function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable. Every step function is integrable. If $f\in\mathcal R$ and $g=f$ a.e., then $g\in\mathcal R$ and $\int g=\int f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Properties:} If $f,g\in\mathcal R[a,b]$, then $f+g$, $cf$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, and $fg$ are all in $\mathcal R$. Also $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\textbf{FTC (4.4,5.3):}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent(1) $F\in C^1[a,b]$, $F'=f$ a.e., $f\in\mathcal R$ $\implies$ $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$. (2) $f\in\mathcal R[a,b]$, $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ $\implies$ $F$ continuous and $F'(x)=f(x)$ a.e.\smallskip

\textbf{MVT for Integrals (5.8):} $f\in\mathcal R[a,b]$, $m\le f\le M$ $\implies\exists c\in[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f=(b-a)f(c)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Differentiating Under Integral (11.4):} $f(x,y)$ continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$ $\implies$ $F(y)=\int_a^b f(x,y)dx$ continuous on $[c,d]$, and if $f_y$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$, then $F'(y)=\int_a^b f_y(x,y)dx$.\smallskip

\section*{Ch12. Lebesgue Measure}
\textbf{Outer Measure $m^*$:} For $E\subset\mathbb R$, $m^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum|I_j|:\cup I_j\supset E,\ \{I_j\}\text{ countable open intervals}\right\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Measurable (Carathéodory, 7.2):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ is Lebesgue measurable $\iff$ $m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ $\forall A\subset\mathbb R$. Equivalently: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ open $U\supset E$ with $m^*(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Measure $m$:} $m(E)=m^*(E)$ for all measurable $E$. All open sets, closed sets, intervals, Borel sets are measurable. $\mathbb Q$, countable sets, null sets are measurable with $m(E)=0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Defs (Functions/Integral):}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$E\subset\mathbb R$ has measure zero ($m(E)=0$): $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ countable cover $\{I_j\}$ with $\sum|I_j|<\varepsilon$. Almost everywhere (a.e.): property holds a.e. if the set where it fails has measure zero. $f$ Lebesgue measurable: $\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $\{f>\alpha\}$ is measurable (equivalently $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$). Lebesgue integral: $\int_E f=\sup\{\int_E\phi:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ simple}\}$. $f\in L^1$: $|f|$ integrable ($\int|f|<\infty$). For $f$ possibly signed: $\int f=\int f^+-\int f^-$, defined when $\int|f|<\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $f_n=\mathbf1_{[n,n+1]}$, $\int f_n=1$ but $f_n\to0$ ptwise. Lebesgue integral still $0$. $\sum f_n=\infty$ on $[0,\infty)$ but finite a.e. at each point — MCT gives $\int\sum f_n=\sum\int f_n=\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Null Sets (7.2):} Every countable set has measure zero. Finite/countable union of null sets is null. $m(E)=0\implies E$ is measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Properties of Measurable Sets (7.3):} $\sigma$-algebra: $E$ meas. $\implies$ $E^c$ meas.; countable unions $\cup E_k$, countable intersections $\cap E_k$ of meas. sets are meas. (hence all Borel sets are meas.). $m(\varnothing)=0$, $m((a,b))=b-a$. Finite additivity: $E\cap F=\varnothing$ $\implies$ $m(E\cup F)=m(E)+m(F)$. Countable additivity: $\{E_k\}$ disjoint $\implies$ $m(\cup E_k)=\sum m(E_k)$. Continuity from below/above: $E_k\uparrow E$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\uparrow m(E)$; $E_k\downarrow E$, $m(E_1)<\infty$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\downarrow m(E)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties (7.1):} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli Lemma (7.5):} $\sum m(\Omega_k)<\infty$ $\implies$ $x\in\Omega_k$ for infinitely many $k$ has measure zero (i.e., a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $\Omega_k$).\smallskip

\textbf{Monotone Convergence (MCT, 11.23):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable, $f_k\uparrow f$ a.e. $\implies\int f_k\uparrow\int f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dominated Convergence (DCT, 11.30):} If: (1) $f_k\to f$ a.e.; (2) $|f_k|\le g$ for all $k$ a.e.; (3) $g\in L^1$ ($\int|g|<\infty$) — then $\int f_k\to\int f$ and $f\in L^1$. (Most commonly used.)\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (DCT):} $f_n=n\mathbf1_{[0,1/n]}$: $f_n\to0$ a.e., $|f_n|\le g$ with $g\equiv1\in L^1$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Fatou's Lemma (11.25):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable $\implies\int\liminf f_k\le\liminf\int f_k$.\smallskip

\textbf{Riemann $\iff$ Lebesgue + Measure Zero (9.49):} For bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$: $f$ Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e., and the two integrals agree.\smallskip

\textbf{$L^p$ Spaces (11.43):} $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. H\"older: $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Minkowski: $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral Properties (11.33):} Let $f,g\in L^1(\Omega)$. Then: (1) linearity: $\int(cf+g)=c\int f+\int g$ for any $c\in\mathbb R$; (2) if $f\le g$ a.e. then $\int f\le\int g$; (3) if $f=g$ a.e. then $\int f=\int g$; (4) $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Integral (11.34):} $f_k\in L^1$, $f_k\to f$ a.e., $|f_k|\le g$ with $g\in L^1$ $\implies$ $f\in L^1$ and $\int f_k\to\int f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e. (11.35):} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e. (set $\{f=\infty\}$ has measure zero).\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity/Measurability of Composite (11.18):} $f$ measurable, $g$ continuous $\implies$ $g\circ f$ measurable. $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ measurable $\iff$ each $f_j$ measurable. $f$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ measurable $\forall a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Almost everywhere modification (11.19):} $f$ Lebesgue measurable, $g=f$ a.e. $\implies$ $g$ is Lebesgue measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Measurable Functions (11.18):} $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ measurable, $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$.\smallskip

\end{multicols}

\medskip

\textbf{P1.} Let $\Omega\subset\R^n$ be measurable and $f:\Omega\to\R^m$.
We show $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$ $\iff$ $f$ measurable.

\medskip
\noindent($\Rightarrow$) Let $V\subset\R^m$ be open. Since open sets are countable unions of open boxes, write $V=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty B_k$ with each $B_k$ an open box. Then
$f^{-1}(V)=f^{-1}\bigl(\bigcup_k B_k\bigr)=\bigcup_k f^{-1}(B_k)$,
a countable union of measurable sets, hence measurable.

\medskip
\noindent($\Leftarrow$) Conversely, if $f$ is measurable, then for any open $V\subset\R^m$, $f^{-1}(V)$ is measurable by definition. Since every open box is open, the condition holds.

\medskip

\textbf{P2.} Let $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m):\Omega\to\R^m$.

\medskip
\noindent($\Rightarrow$) If $f$ is measurable and $B\subset\R$ is open, then $f^{-1}(B\times\R^{m-1})=f_1^{-1}(B)$ is measurable (open box in $\R^m$). Similarly for each $f_j$.

\medskip
\noindent($\Leftarrow$) If each $f_j$ is measurable, let $V\subset\R^m$ be open. Write $V=\bigcup_k B_k$ as a countable union of open boxes. Then
$f^{-1}(B_k)=\bigcap_{j=1}^m f_j^{-1}(B_{k,j})$ where $B_{k,j}$ is the $j$-th projection of $B_k$, an open interval in $\R$. Each $f_j^{-1}(B_{k,j})$ is measurable, hence their intersection is measurable, and countable union over $k$ is measurable.

\medskip

\textbf{P3.} Let $f:\Omega\to W$ be measurable and $g:W\to\R^p$ be continuous.

For any open $U\subset\R^p$, since $g$ is continuous, $g^{-1}(U)$ is open in $W$, hence open in $\R^m$ (since $W$ is open). Thus
$(g\circ f)^{-1}(U)=f^{-1}(g^{-1}(U))$
is the preimage of an open set under $f$, which is measurable. Hence $g\circ f$ is measurable.

\medskip

\textbf{P4.} Let $f:\Omega\to\R$.

\medskip
\noindent($\Rightarrow$) If $f$ is measurable, then for any $a\in\R$, $(a,\infty)$ is open, so $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ is measurable.

\medskip
\noindent($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ is measurable for every $a\in\R$. Every open set $V\subset\R$ can be written as a countable union of open intervals:
$V=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty(a_k,b_k)=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty\bigl((a_k,\infty)\setminus[b_k,\infty)\bigr)$.
Since $[b,\infty)=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty(b-n^{-1},\infty)$, it is a countable intersection of measurable sets, hence measurable. So $V$ is a countable union of measurable sets, thus measurable. Hence $f^{-1}(V)$ is measurable for every open $V$, so $f$ is measurable.

\medskip

\textbf{P5.} Let $f$ be Lebesgue measurable and $g=f$ a.e. on $\R^n\setminus A$ where $m(A)=0$.

For any open $V\subset\R$, either $V$ is empty (trivial) or $V\neq\varnothing$. We have
$g^{-1}(V)=\bigl(g^{-1}(V)\cap(\R^n\setminus A)\bigr)\cup\bigl(g^{-1}(V)\cap A\bigr)$.
Since $g=f$ on $\R^n\setminus A$, $g^{-1}(V)\cap(\R^n\setminus A)=f^{-1}(V)\cap(\R^n\setminus A)$, which is a measurable set minus a null set, hence measurable. Also $A$ has measure zero, so $g^{-1}(V)\cap A$ has measure zero and is therefore measurable. Their union is measurable. Thus $g$ is measurable.

\medskip

\textbf{P6.} Let $A$ be an open interval in $\R$. Then $A\cap(0,\infty)$ and $A\setminus(0,\infty)=A\cap(-\infty,0]$ are disjoint and their union is $A$. By definition of outer measure as infimum,
\[m^*(A\cap(0,\infty))+m^*(A\setminus(0,\infty))\le m^*(A),\]
since the cover of $A$ by intervals also covers the two pieces. Conversely, any cover of $A\cap(0,\infty)$ and $A\setminus(0,\infty)$ by intervals is also a cover of $A$, so
$m^*(A)\le m^*(A\cap(0,\infty))+m^*(A\setminus(0,\infty)).$
Thus equality holds.

\medskip

\textbf{P7.} Let $A=(a_1,b_1)\times(a_2,b_2)$ be an open box in $\R^2$ and $E=\{(x_1,x_2):x_2>0\}$ the upper half-plane. Then $A\cap E$ and $A\setminus E$ are disjoint open rectangles (possibly empty). By the same argument as P6,
\[m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)\le m^*(A),\]
and
\[m^*(A)\le m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E),\]
since any cover of $A$ covers both pieces. Hence equality holds.

\medskip

\textbf{P8.} We show $E=\{(x_1,x_2):x_2>0\}$ satisfies the Carathéodory condition.

Let $A\subset\R^2$ be arbitrary. If $A\cap E=\varnothing$ or $A\setminus E=\varnothing$, the condition is trivial. Otherwise, consider any cover $\{B_j\}$ of $A$ by open boxes. Then $\{B_j\cap E\}$ covers $A\cap E$ and $\{B_j\setminus E\}$ covers $A\setminus E$. Therefore
\[\sum_j\operatorname{vol}(B_j)\ge\sum_j\operatorname{vol}(B_j\cap E)+\sum_j\operatorname{vol}(B_j\setminus E)\ge m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E).\]
Taking infimum over all covers gives $m^*(A)\ge m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$. Since outer measure is always countably subadditive, the reverse inequality holds. Hence $E$ is measurable.

\medskip

\textbf{P9.} Since $A$ is measurable, $m^*(T)=m^*(T\cap A)+m^*(T\setminus A)$ for all $T\subset\R^n$. Take $T=B$. Then
\[m^*(B)=m^*(B\cap A)+m^*(B\setminus A).\]
But $B\setminus A$ and $A\setminus B$ have the same outer measure by hypothesis (both equal $m^*(B\setminus A)=m^*(A\setminus B)=0$). Moreover, $B\cap A\subset A$ and $A\setminus B\subset B$, so
$m^*(B\cap A)\le m^*(A)=m(A)$ and $m^*(B\setminus A)\le m^*(A\setminus B)=0$.
Thus $m^*(B)=m^*(B\cap A)\le m^*(A)$. Also $m^*(B)\ge m^*(B\cap A)$ trivially.

To verify the Carathéodory condition for $B$: for any $T$,
\begin{align*}
m^*(T)&=m^*(T\cap A)+m^*(T\setminus A)\\
&=m^*(T\cap A\cap B)+m^*(T\cap A\setminus B)+m^*(T\setminus A\cap B)+m^*(T\setminus(A\cup B))\\
&\ge m^*(T\cap B)+m^*(T\setminus B),
\end{align*}
since each term on the right is $\le$ the corresponding term on the left (set inclusion). Thus $B$ is measurable.

\medskip

\textbf{P10.} Let $E\subset\R^n$.

\medskip
\noindent($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $E$ is measurable. If $E=\R^n$, trivial. Otherwise, for any $\varepsilon>0$, by the regularity property of Lebesgue measure, there exists an open set $U\supset E$ with $m(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.

\medskip
\noindent($\Leftarrow$) Conversely, suppose for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is open $U_\varepsilon\supset E$ with $m^*(U_\varepsilon\setminus E)<\varepsilon$. Write $U_k=U_{1/k}$ for $k\in\N$. Then $E\subset\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty U_k$, and
\[m^*\!\Bigl(\bigcap_k U_k\setminus E\Bigr)\le m^*(U_k\setminus E)<\frac1k\quad\forall k,\]
so $m^*(\bigcap_k U_k\setminus E)=0$. Let $G=\bigcap_k U_k$; then $G$ is a countable intersection of open sets, hence a $G_\delta$ set, and $G$ is measurable (all Borel sets are measurable). Since $E\subset G$ and $G\setminus E$ has measure zero, $E=G\setminus(G\setminus E)$ is measurable (difference of a measurable set and a null set).

\end{document}

\textbf{Simple Functions (8.1):} $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ simple if $f(\Omega)$ finite. Every simple $f=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\chi_{E_j}$ with $E_j$ disjoint, measurable. $\chi_E$ is characteristic/indicator function.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral of Simple (8.1.6):} $f\ge0$ simple: $\int_\Omega f:=\sum_{\lambda\in f(\Omega),\lambda>0}\lambda\,m(\{x\in\Omega:f(x)=\lambda\})$. Equivalently $\int_\Omega\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}=\sum c_j m(E_j)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Basic Properties (8.1.10):} $0\le\int f\le\infty$; $\int f=0\iff f=0$ a.e.; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $\int cf=c\int f$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (simple integral):} $f=3\chi_{[1,2]}+4\chi_{(2,4]}$, $\int f=3\cdot m([1,2])+4\cdot m((2,4])=3\cdot1+4\cdot2=11$. $g=1_{[0,\infty)}$, $\int g=+\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral of Non-neg Functions (8.2.2):} $f:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ measurable: $\int_\Omega f:=\sup\{\int_\Omega s:0\le s\le f,\ s\text{ simple}\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{MCT (8.2.9):} $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, $f_n\uparrow f$ a.e. $\implies\int f_n\uparrow\int f$. (Key: can interchange limit and integral for monotone seq.)\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (MCT):} $\int_{[0,1]}\sum_{k=1}^n\chi_{[k-1,k)}/k^2=\sum_{k=1}^\infty1/k^2=\pi^2/6$ by MCT.\smallskip

\textbf{Fatou (8.2.13):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable $\implies\int\liminf f_k\le\liminf\int f_k$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1)}$, $\liminf f_n=0$, $\int\liminf=0$, $\liminf\int f_n=1$, strict inequality. MCT needs increasing; Fatou works for any non-neg.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli (8.2.15):} $\sum m(E_k)<\infty\implies$ a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $E_k$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum1/k^2<\infty$, so a.e. $x\in[0,1]$ lies in only finitely many intervals $(q_k-1/k^2,q_k+1/k^2)$ covering rationals.\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Integrable (8.3.1):} $f$ measurable, $\int_\Omega|f|<\infty$. Write $f=f^+-f^-$, $|f|=f^++f^-$. $\int_\Omega f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$. Note: $\int_\Omega|f^+|,\int_\Omega|f^-|<\infty$, so no $+\infty-(+\infty)$. Also $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (abs integrable):} $f(x)=\sin x/x$ on $[0,\infty)$ is not abs integrable ($\int_1^\infty|\sin x/x|dx=+\infty$), so not in $L^1$. But $f(x)=e^{-x^2}$ on $\mathbb R$ is abs integrable ($\int e^{-x^2}dx=\sqrt\pi$).\smallskip

\textbf{DCT (8.3.4):} $f_n\to f$ a.e., $|f_n|\le F$ with $F\in L^1$ $\implies\int f_n\to\int f$ and $f\in L^1$. (Most commonly used theorem.)\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (DCT):} $f_n(x)=n\chi_{[0,1/n]}(x)$, $f_n\to0$ a.e., $|f_n|\le1\in L^1$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Properties (8.3.3):} $f,g\in L^1$: $\int cf=c\int f$; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$; $f=g$ a.e. $\implies\int f=\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{Almost everywhere (8.2.6):} $\int f=0\iff f=0$ a.e. $\int_\Omega f<\infty\implies f<\infty$ a.e. (set $\{f=+\infty\}$ has measure zero.)\smallskip

\textbf{Fubini (8.5.1):} $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ abs integrable. Then for a.e. $x$, $f(x,y)$ abs integrable in $y$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^2}f=\int_{\mathbb R}(\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)dy)dx=\int_{\mathbb R}(\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)dx)dy$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Fubini):} $\int_{[0,1]^2}xy\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1(\int_0^1 xy\,dy)dx=\int_0^1(x/2)dx=1/4$. Since $xy\ge0$, Fubini applies directly.\smallskip

\textbf{Riemann $\Rightarrow$ Lebesgue (8.4.1):} $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e., and $\int_{\text{Riem}}f=\int_{\text{Leb}}f$. \textbf{Ex:} Dirichlet's function $f=1_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$: not Riemann integrable but Lebesgue integrable with $\int f=0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Summary: Riemann vs Lebesgue:} Riemann: $\int^-f=\sup\{\int\phi:\phi\le f\}$, Lebesgue: $\int f=\sup\{\int\phi:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ simple}\}$. Both agree on $[a,b]$ for Riemann integrable $f$, but Lebesgue handles more: $1_{\mathbb Q}$, pointwise limits, etc.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Measure $m$:} $m(E)=m^*(E)$ for all measurable $E$. All open sets, closed sets, intervals, Borel sets are measurable. $\mathbb Q$, countable sets, null sets are measurable with $m(E)=0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Defs (Functions/Integral):}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$E\subset\mathbb R$ has measure zero ($m(E)=0$): $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ countable cover $\{I_j\}$ with $\sum|I_j|<\varepsilon$. Almost everywhere (a.e.): property holds a.e. if the set where it fails has measure zero. $f$ Lebesgue measurable: $\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $\{f>\alpha\}$ is measurable (equivalently $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$). Lebesgue integral: $\int_E f=\sup\{\int_E\phi:0\le\phi\le f,\ \phi\text{ simple}\}$. $f\in L^1$: $|f|$ integrable ($\int|f|<\infty$). For $f$ possibly signed: $\int f=\int f^+-\int f^-$, defined when $\int|f|<\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Null Sets (7.4.4f):} Every countable set has measure zero. Finite/countable union of null sets is null. $m(E)=0\implies E$ is measurable (Carathéodory: any null set splits every $A$ perfectly). \textbf{Ex (proving $E$ meas from $m^*E=0$):} If $m^*(E)=0$, for any $A\subset\mathbb R^n$, by subadditivity $m^*(A)\le m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)\le0+m^*(A\setminus E)\le m^*(A)$, so Carathéodory holds.\smallskip

\textbf{Properties of Measurable Sets (7.4.4):} $\sigma$-algebra: $E$ meas. $\implies$ $E^c$ meas.; countable unions/intersections of meas. sets are meas. (hence all Borel sets are meas.). $m(\varnothing)=0$, $m((a,b))=b-a$. Finite additivity: $E\cap F=\varnothing$ $\implies$ $m(E\cup F)=m(E)+m(F)$. Countable additivity: $\{E_k\}$ disjoint $\implies$ $m(\cup E_k)=\sum m(E_k)$. Translation invariance: $m(E+x)=m(E)$. Continuity from below/above: $E_k\uparrow E$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\uparrow m(E)$; $E_k\downarrow E$, $m(E_1)<\infty$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\downarrow m(E)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties (7.2.5):} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$. \textbf{Ex:} $m^*(\mathbb Q)=0$: enumerate $\mathbb Q=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$, cover $q_k$ by interval of length $\varepsilon/2^k$, so $m^*(\mathbb Q)\le\sum\varepsilon/2^k=\varepsilon$. $m^*([0,1])=1$, $m^*([0,1]^2)=1$, $m^*(\text{line in }\mathbb R^2)=0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli Lemma (8.2.15):} $\sum m(\Omega_k)<\infty\implies$ a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $\Omega_k$. \textbf{Ex:} $[0,1]$ covered by $\Omega_n=[0,1/n]$, $m(\Omega_n)=1/n$, $\sum1/n=\infty$: BC doesn't apply, indeed every $x\in(0,1]$ is in infinitely many $\Omega_n$. But if $m(\Omega_n)=1/n^2$, then $\sum1/n^2<\infty$, so a.e. $x$ in only finitely many.\smallskip

\textbf{Existence of Lebesgue Measure (7.1.1):} There exists a concept of measurable set and $m(E)$ obeying: (i) Borel: all open/closed sets measurable; (ii) complement; (iii) countable unions/intersections; (iv) positivity, $0\le m\le\infty$; (v) monotonicity; (vi) finite/countable additivity; (vii) normalization $m([0,1]^n)=1$; (viii) translation invariance. Lebesgue measure is unique among such measures.\smallskip

\textbf{Non-measurable sets (7.3):} Outer measure is not finitely additive. Vitali set: using axiom of choice, partition $\mathbb R$ into cosets of $\mathbb Q$, pick one representative from each coset in $[0,1]$. This set is not Lebesgue measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity/Measurability of Composite (7.5.5):} $f$ measurable, $g$ continuous $\implies$ $g\circ f$ measurable. $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ measurable $\iff$ each $f_j$ measurable. $f$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ measurable $\forall a$ (7.5.8). Continuous functions are measurable (7.5.2).\smallskip

\textbf{Almost everywhere modification (7.5.5):} $f$ Lebesgue measurable, $g=f$ a.e. $\implies$ $g$ is Lebesgue measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Riemann $\iff$ Lebesgue + Measure Zero (8.4.1):} For bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$: $f$ Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e., and the two integrals agree.\smallskip

\textbf{$L^p$ Spaces (in Tao):} $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. H\"older: $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Minkowski: $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\smallskip

\textbf{$L^p$ Spaces (11.43):} $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. H\"older: $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Minkowski: $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral Properties (11.33):} Let $f,g\in L^1(\Omega)$. Then: (1) linearity: $\int(cf+g)=c\int f+\int g$ for any $c\in\mathbb R$; (2) if $f\le g$ a.e. then $\int f\le\int g$; (3) if $f=g$ a.e. then $\int f=\int g$; (4) $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Integral (11.34):} $f_k\in L^1$, $f_k\to f$ a.e., $|f_k|\le g$ with $g\in L^1$ $\implies$ $f\in L^1$ and $\int f_k\to\int f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e. (11.35):} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e. (set $\{f=\infty\}$ has measure zero).\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity/Measurability of Composite (11.18):} $f$ measurable, $g$ continuous $\implies$ $g\circ f$ measurable. $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ measurable $\iff$ each $f_j$ measurable. $f$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ measurable $\forall a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Almost everywhere modification (11.19):} $f$ Lebesgue measurable, $g=f$ a.e. $\implies$ $g$ is Lebesgue measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity of Lebesgue Measurable Functions (11.18):} $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ measurable, $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$.\smallskip

\end{multicols}

\documentclass[8pt]{extarticle}
\usepackage[margin=0.15in, landscape, top=0.12in, bottom=0.12in, left=0.12in, right=0.12in]{geometry}

\begin{document}
\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\fontsize{6pt}{7.5pt}\selectfont
\addtolength{\baselineskip}{-1.5pt}
