\begin{multicols}{3}

\section*{Ch6. Infinite Series of Real Numbers}
\textbf{Defs:} $s_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k$. $\sum a_k$ converges to $s$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|s_n-s|<\varepsilon$. Diverges: $\{s_n\}$ has no limit. Abs conv: $\sum|a_k|<\infty$. Conditional: conv but not abs.\smallskip

\textbf{Divergence Test (6.5):} $a_k\not\to0\implies\sum a_k$ diverges. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum\sin k$: $a_k=\sin k\not\to0$, diverges.\smallskip

\textbf{Geometric (6.7):} $\sum_{k=0}^\infty x^k=\frac1{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$, diverges for $|x|\ge1$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum(1/2)^k=1$, $\sum(-1)^k$ diverges, $\sum 1^k$ diverges.\smallskip

\textbf{Cauchy Criterion (6.8):} $\sum a_k$ conv $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:m\ge n\ge N\implies\sum_{k=n}^m a_k<\varepsilon$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum(-1)^k/k$ satisfies Cauchy, converges (conditionally).\smallskip

\textbf{Comparison (6.14):} $0\le a_k\le b_k$ for large $k$: $\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$; $\sum a_k=\infty\implies\sum b_k=\infty$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum1/(k^2+1)$ conv since $\le\sum1/k^2$.\smallskip

\textbf{LCT (6.16):} $L=\lim a_k/b_k$, $b_k>0$. $0<L<\infty$: same conv. $L=0$+$\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$. $L=\infty$+$\sum b_k=\infty\implies\sum a_k=\infty$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum k/(k^2+1)$ vs $\sum1/k$: $L=\lim(k/(k^2+1))/(1/k)=1$, so same conv as $\sum1/k$ (diverges).\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Test (6.12):} $f\ge0$ decr on $[1,\infty)$. $\sum f(k)$ conv $\iff\int_1^\infty f<\infty$. $\sum1/k^p$ conv $\iff p>1$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum1/k\log k$ diverges ($f(x)=1/(x\log x)$, $\int_2^\infty dx/(x\log x)=\infty$). $\sum1/(k\log^2k)$ conv.\smallskip

\textbf{Root Test (6.23):} $r=\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum(1/2)^k$: $r=1/2<1$, conv. $\sum 2^k$: $r=2>1$, diverges.\smallskip

\textbf{Ratio Test (6.24):} $r=\lim|a_{k+1}/a_k|$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $\sum k/e^k$ conv by ratio test ($r=1/e<1$). $\sum k^2/(k+1)$ diverges ($a_k\to\infty$). $\sum1/k^2$ conv ($p=2>1$). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond conv ($|a_k|=1/k$, abs diverges).\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Conv (6.20):} Abs conv $\implies$conv (converse false). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Rearrangements (6.27):} If $\sum a_k$ abs conv, every rearrangement $\to$ same sum. Cond conv $\implies$ can rearrange to any $x\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abel's Formula (6.30):} $A_{n,m}=\sum_{k=m}^n a_k$. $\sum_{k=m}^n a_kb_k=A_{n,m}b_n-\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}A_{k,m}(b_{k+1}-b_k)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test (6.31):} $\sum a_k$ partial sums bounded + $b_k\downarrow0$ $\implies\sum a_kb_k$ converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Alt Series Test (6.32):} $a_k\downarrow0\implies\sum(-1)^ka_k$ converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Alt Series Error (6.38):} $a_k\downarrow0$, $s=\sum(-1)^ka_k$, $|s-s_n|\le a_{n+1}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Test Error (6.35):} $0\le\sum_{k=1}^n f(k)-\int_1^n f\le f(1)$. If $\sum f(k)$ conv: $0\le s-s_n+\int_n^\infty f\le f(n)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Logarithmic Test (6.42):} $p=\lim\frac{\log(1/|a_k|)}{\log k}$. $p>1\implies$abs conv; $p<1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Raabe's Test (6.43):} $|a_{k+1}/a_k|\le1-p/k+O(1/k)$ with $p>1\implies\sum a_k$ abs conv.\smallskip

\section*{Ch7. Infinite Series of Functions}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f_n\to f$ ptwise: $\forall x\in E$, $\lim f_n(x)=f(x)$. $f_n\to f$ uniformly: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$ ($N$ depends only on $\varepsilon$). Radius of conv $R$: abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (7.9):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ cont at $x_0\in E$ $\implies f$ cont at $x_0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Integrability (7.10):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$, each integrable $\implies f$ integrable and $\int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n/n$ on $[0,1]$, uniform conv since $|x^n/n|\le1/n\to0$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0=\int_0^1 f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Boundedness + Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} $f_n$ uniformly bounded on $E$ ($\exists M:|f_n(x)|\le M$ $\forall n,x$) + $f_n\to f$ uniformly $\implies f$ bounded on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$ and each $f_n$ bounded on $E$, then $f$ is bounded on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Product of Uniformly Conv Functions:} If: (1) $f_n\to f$, $g_n\to g$ uniformly on $E$; (2) $f,g$ bounded on $E$ — then $f_ng_n\to fg$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cesàro Mean:} If $b_k\to b$, then $\frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}\to b$. Equivalently, Stolz-Cesàro: if $c_n\to c$ and $a_n$ monotone or $d_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\to\infty$, then $\lim\frac{a_n}{d_n}=L\implies\lim\frac{\sum a_k}{\sum d_k}=L$.\smallskip

\textbf{Arith. Mean Conv:} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ bounded $\implies$ $\frac{f_1+\dots+f_n}{n}\to f$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Differentiability (7.12):} (1) $(a,b)$ bounded; (2) each $f_n$ diff on $(a,b)$; (3) $f_n(x_0)\to L$ for some $x_0$; (4) $f_n'$ converges uniformly on $(a,b)$ $\implies$ $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $(a,b)$ and $f'=\lim f_n'$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n/n$ on $(0,1)$: $f_n'=|x|^{n-1}$, not uniform on $(0,1)$ (diverges at $x\to1$), so thm doesn't apply.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Cauchy Criterion (7.11):} $f_n$ conv uniformly on $E$ $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n,m\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n/n$, $|f_n-f_m|\le|x^n/n|+|x^m/m|\le1/n+1/m\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$, so conv uniformly.\smallskip

\textbf{Weierstrass M-Test (7.15):} $|f_k(x)|\le M_k$ for $x\in E$, $\sum M_k<\infty\implies\sum f_k$ abs conv and uniformly on $E$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum x^k/k$, $|x|^k/k\le1/k$ on $[0,1]$, $\sum1/k=\infty$ so M-test fails on $[0,1]$. But on $[0,r]$, $r<1$, M-test works ($\sum r^k/k<\infty$).\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Diff (7.14):} (1) $I$ open interval; (2) each $f_k$ differentiable on $I$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges at some $x_0\in I$; (4) $\sum f_k'$ converges uniformly on $I$ $\implies$ $(\sum f_k)'=\sum f_k'$ on $I$.\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Int (7.14):} (1) $[a,b]$ closed; (2) each $f_k$ integrable on $[a,b]$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges uniformly on $[a,b]$ $\implies$ $\int_a^b\sum f_k=\sum\int_a^b f_k$.\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Cont (7.14):} (1) $E$ set; (2) each $f_k$ continuous on $E$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges uniformly on $E$ $\implies$ $\sum f_k$ continuous on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test for Uniform Conv (7.16):} $|\sum_{k=1}^n f_k(x)|\le M$ for all $n,x\in E$ and $g_k\downarrow0$ uniformly $\implies\sum f_kg_k$ converges uniformly. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum\frac{\sin kx}{k}$ on $[0,2\pi]$: partial sums of $\sin kx$ are uniformly bounded (by $1/|\sin(x/2)|$ but bounded on $[0,2\pi]\setminus\{0\}$), $1/k\downarrow0$ uniformly, so uniform conv on $[0,2\pi]\setminus\{0\}$ (actually on any $[a,2\pi-a]$, $a>0$).\smallskip

\textbf{Power Series Radius (7.21):} $S(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$, $R=1/\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $S$ abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, uniformly on any $[a,b]\subset(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum x^k/k$: $a_k=1/k$, $R=1$. On $(-1,1)$ abs conv; at $x=1$, harmonic series diverges; at $x=-1$, alternating series converges.\smallskip

\textbf{PS Diff \& Int (7.26,7.32):} On $(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, $S\in C^\infty$ and $S'(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty k a_k(x-x_0)^{k-1}$, $\int S=\sum\frac{a_k}{k+1}(x-x_0)^{k+1}+C$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abel's Theorem (7.27):} If $\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ converges on $[a,b]$, then it converges uniformly on $[a,b]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniqueness (7.39):} If $f(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ on open interval $I$, then $a_k=f^{(k)}(x_0)/k!$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$: ptwise $f_n\to0$ for $x<1$, $f_n(1)=1$, so not continuous at $x=1$ (non-uniform). $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,r]$, $r<1$: uniform conv (M-test: $M_k=r^k$, $\sum r^k<\infty$). $f_n(x)=x^n(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$: uniform conv by M-test ($x^n(1-x)\le 1$).\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (proving non-uniform):} To show $f_n(x)=1/(nx)\to0$ not uniform on $(0,1)$: negation says $\exists\varepsilon>0$ s.t. $\forall N$, $\exists n\ge N$, $\exists x\in(0,1)$ with $|1/(nx)-0|\ge\varepsilon$. Take $\varepsilon=1$, pick $x=1/n$, then $|1/(n\cdot1/n)|=1\ge1$. QED.\smallskip

\section*{Ch8. Euclidean Spaces $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent Open ball: $B_r(a)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x-a\|<r\}$. Closed ball: $\{\|x-a\|\le r\}$. $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ is \textbf{open}: $\forall a\in V$, $\exists\varepsilon>0:B_\varepsilon(a)\subset V$. $E$ is \textbf{closed}: $E^c$ is open. \textbf{Relatively open in} $A$: $E\subset A$ is relatively open if $E=A\cap V$ for some open $V$. \textbf{Relatively closed in} $A$: $E=A\cap F$ for some closed $F$. \textbf{Compact}: every open cover has a finite subcover. \textbf{Connected}: cannot be separated into two nonempty disjoint relatively-open sets. \textbf{Interior} $E^\circ$: union of all open subsets of $E$ (largest open set $\subset E$). \textbf{Closure} $\overline{E}$: intersection of all closed supersets of $E$ (smallest closed set $\supset E$). \textbf{Boundary} $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$. \textbf{Limit point}: $x$ is limit point of $E$ if every $B_\varepsilon(x)$ contains $y\in E$ with $y\ne x$. $E$ is \textbf{perfect}: $E$ is closed and every point of $E$ is a limit point of $E$. \textbf{Dense}: $\overline{E}=\mathbb R^n$ (or $\overline{E}\cap U\neq\varnothing$ for every open $U$).\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $\mathbb Q$ is dense in $\mathbb R$. $(0,1)$ is open, not closed. $[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q$ is not closed, not open. $\mathbb R^n$ is connected. $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ is connected. Cantor set is perfect and nowhere dense.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (proving open/closed):} To show $V=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:s<\|x-a\|<r\}$ is open: for any $y\in V$, set $\varepsilon=\min\{s-\|y-a\|,\|y-a\|-r\}>0$. Then $B_\varepsilon(y)\subset V$. To show $E=\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is closed: complement $E^c=\{x:\|x-a\|>r\}$ is open (similar argument). Shell is neither: boundary points satisfy equality.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (counterexamples):} $(A\cup B)^\circ\neq A^\circ\cup B^\circ$: take $A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$, then $(A\cup B)^\circ=(0,2)$ but $A^\circ\cup B^\circ=(0,1)\cup(1,2)$. $\overline{A\cap B}\neq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$: take $A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$, then $\overline{A\cap B}=\overline{\varnothing}=\varnothing$ but $\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}=[0,1]\cap[1,2]=\{1\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cauchy-Schwarz (8.5):} $|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, equality $\iff x,y$ parallel or one is zero. \textbf{Ex:} In $\mathbb R^2$, $(1,1)\cdot(2,3)=5$, $\|(1,1)\|=\sqrt2$, $\|(2,3)\|=\sqrt{13}$, so $5\le\sqrt{26}$, equality when $(1,1)=\lambda(2,3)$ (no real $\lambda$).\smallskip

\textbf{Triangle Inequalities (8.6):} $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$, $\|x-y\|\ge|\|x\|-\|y\||$. \textbf{Ex:} $x=(1,2)$, $y=(3,1)$: $\|x+y\|=\|(4,3)\|=5$, $\|x\|+\|y\|=\sqrt5+\sqrt{10}\approx5.4\ge5$.\smallskip

\textbf{Norm Inequalities (8.7):} $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$, $\|x\|\le\|x\|_1\le\sqrt n\|x\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cross Product (8.9):} $x,y\in\mathbb R^3$: $x\times y\perp x$ and $x\times y\perp y$. $\|x\times y\|=\|x\|\|y\|\sin\theta$. $x\times(y\times z)=(x\cdot z)y-(x\cdot y)z$.\smallskip

\textbf{Balls are Open/Closed (8.21):} Open ball $B_r(a)$ is open; closed ball $\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is closed. Shell $\{x:s\le\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is neither open nor closed.\smallskip

\textbf{Open/Closed Properties (8.24):} Arbitrary unions of open are open; finite intersections of open are open. Arbitrary intersections of closed are closed; finite unions of closed are closed.\smallskip

\textbf{Relatively Open/Closed (8.26):} If $C\subset E\subset\mathbb R^n$: (1) $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ relatively open in $E$. (2) $C$ relatively open in $E$ + $E$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$.\smallskip

\textbf{Connected $\iff$ Interval (8.30):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ connected $\iff$ $E$ is an interval. Rectangles in $\mathbb R^n$ are connected.\smallskip

\textbf{Interior, Closure, Boundary (8.31,8.34):} Interior $E^\circ$ is largest open $\subset E$; closure $\overline{E}$ is smallest closed $\supset E$; boundary $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$.\smallskip

\textbf{Closure/Interior Monotonicity (8.37):} $A\subset B$ $\implies$ $\overline{A}\subset\overline{B}$ and $A^\circ\subset B^\circ$.\smallskip

\textbf{Boundary Thm (8.36):} $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$. Also $\overline{E}=E^\circ\cup\partial E$, disjoint.\smallskip

\textbf{Interior/Closure of Subsets:} If $U\subset E$ relatively open in $E$: (1) If $U\subset E^\circ$, then $U\cap\partial E=\varnothing$. (2) If $U\cap\partial E\neq\varnothing$, then $U\cap\partial U=U\cap\partial E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Linear Maps (8.15-8.18):} $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ linear $\iff$ $T(x)=Bx$ for unique $m\times n$ matrix $B$. Operator norm: $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\neq0}\frac{\|T(x)\|}{\|x\|}$, and $\|T(x)\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Distance Between Sets (8.33):} $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{\|x-y\|:x\in A,y\in B\}$. If $A,B$ are compact and disjoint, then $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$.\smallskip

\section*{Ch9. Convergence in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\dots,x_k^{(n)})\to a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\iff x_k^{(j)}\to a_j$ for each $j$. Bounded: $\exists M>0:\|x_k\|\le M\ \forall k$. Cauchy: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:k,m\ge N\implies\|x_k-x_m\|<\varepsilon$. $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to a$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists\delta>0:0<\|x-a\|<\delta\implies\|f(x)-L\|<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Conv $\iff$ Componentwise (9.2):} $x_k^{(j)}\to a_j\ \forall j\iff x_k\to a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Sequence Properties (9.4,9.6):} Uniqueness. Subseq $\to$ same limit. Conv $\implies$ bounded. Conv $\iff$ Cauchy.\smallskip

\textbf{Bolzano-Weierstrass (9.5):} Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb R^n$ has a convergent subsequence. \textbf{Ex:} $x_k=(\sin k,\cos k)$ bounded in $\mathbb R^2$, has conv subseq by BW.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit Laws (9.15):} $\lim(f+g)=L+M$, $\lim(\alpha f)=\alpha L$, $\lim(f\cdot g)=L\cdot M$. Squeeze: $g\le h\le f$, $\lim f=\lim g=L\implies\lim h=L$. Composition: $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L$, $\lim_{y\to L}h(y)=M\implies\lim_{x\to a}h(g(x))=M$.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit $\iff$ Sequential (9.15ii):} $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\iff f(x_k)\to L$ for every $x_k\to a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous $\iff$ Preimage of Open (9.26):} $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\iff$ $f^{-1}(V)$ relatively open in $E$ for every open $V\subset\mathbb R^m$.\smallskip

\textbf{Compact $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (9.29):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous on $K$ $\implies f(K)$ compact. Hence $f$ bounded and attains max/min (Extreme Value Thm 9.32).\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity $\Rightarrow$ Connectedness (9.30):} $E$ connected, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f(E)$ is connected.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous Inverse (9.33):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ is 1-1 and continuous $\implies f^{-1}$ continuous on $f(K)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Continuity on Compact (9.25):} $E$ compact, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f$ uniformly continuous.\smallskip

\textbf{Dini's Theorem (9.40):} $K$ compact, $f_k:K\to\mathbb R$ ptwise monotone to continuous $f$ $\implies f_k\to f$ uniformly on $K$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Continuity $\iff$ Coord-wise (9.18):} $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m):E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous at $a$ $\iff$ each $f_j$ is continuous at $a$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Dot Product Conv (9.22):} $x_k\to0$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $y_k$ bounded in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $x_k\cdot y_k\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Heine-Borel (9.11):} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ compact $\iff$ $E$ is closed and bounded.\smallskip

\textbf{Closed $\iff$ Sequential (9.8):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $x_k\in E$, $x_k\to x$ $\implies x\in E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit Point Char (9.7):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $E$ contains all its limit points.\smallskip

\textbf{Compact + Isolated Points $\implies$ Finite (9.12):} $K$ compact, each $x\in K$ isolated ($\exists r>0:B_r(x)\cap K=\{x\}$) $\implies$ $K$ is finite.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (proving no limit):} To show $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ DNE: along $y=x$ gives $1/2$, along $y=0$ gives $0$. Since $1/2\neq0$, limit DNE.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel Covering (9.9):} Every open cover of a compact set has a finite subcover.\smallskip

\section*{Ch11. Differentiability on $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs (11.1,11.12):}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f:V\to\mathbb R^m$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open. $f$ diff at $a\in V$ $\iff$ $\exists$ linear $Df(a):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ s.t. $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Df(a)h\|}{\|h\|}=0$. $Df(a)$ = Jacobian (total derivative). If $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$, then $Df=(J_{ij})$, $J_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$. $f\in C^p$: all partials of order $\le p$ exist and are continuous.\smallskip

\textbf{Differentiability $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (11.13):} $f$ diff at $a$ $\implies$ all partials exist and $f$ continuous at $a$. But partials exist $\not\Rightarrow$ diff.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (not diff):} $f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$, $f(0,0)=0$. $f_x(0,0)=0$, $f_y(0,0)=0$, but not diff at $(0,0)$. Proof: with $h=(t,t)$, ratio $=1/2\not\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous Partials $\Rightarrow$ Diff (11.15):} If all $\partial f/\partial x_j$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of $a$, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Equality of Mixed Partials (11.2):} If $f\in C^1$, and one mixed partial $f_{xy}$ or $f_{yx}$ exists and is continuous at $(a,b)$, then $f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b)$. In particular, if $f\in C^2$, then $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Derivative Rules (11.20):} Sum, scalar multiple, product, quotient rules all hold for the total derivative $D$. $(Df\cdot Dg)(x)=Df(x)\cdot Dg(x)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Chain Rule (11.28):} $D(f\circ g)(a)=Df(g(a))Dg(a)$. Scalar: $\partial f/\partial x_i=\sum_j\frac{\partial f}{\partial u_j}\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}$. \textbf{Ex:} $f(u)=e^u$, $u=g(x)=x^2$, so $(f\circ g)'=e^{x^2}\cdot2x$.\smallskip

\textbf{Tangent Hyperplane (11.21):} If $f:V\to\mathbb R$ diff at $a$, the tangent hyperplane to the graph at $(a,f(a))$ is $y=f(a)+Df(a)(x-a)$. The surface is differentiable at $a$ iff the graph has a tangent hyperplane there.\smallskip

\textbf{Mean Value Inequality (11.30):} $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, connected; $f:U\to\mathbb R$ diff; $\|Df(x)\|\le M$ $\forall x\in U$ $\implies$ $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|$ $\forall x,y\in U$.\smallskip

\textbf{Convex MVT (11.32):} $U$ convex, $f:U\to\mathbb R^m$ diff: $\exists c\in U$ with $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le\|Df(c)\|\|x-y\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Taylor's Theorem (11.37):} $f\in C^{k+1}$: $f(b)=f(a)+\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{j!}(D^jf(a))(b-a)^j+\frac1{(k+1)!}(D^{k+1}f(c))(b-a)^{k+1}$ for some $c$ on $[a,b]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Taylor 2nd Order, 2 vars (11.59):} $f(a+h,b+k)=f(a,b)+hf_x+kf_y+\frac12(h^2f_{xx}+2hkf_{xy}+k^2f_{yy})+o(h^2+k^2)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Inverse Function Theorem (11.41):} $f:V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, $f\in C^1$, $a\in V$, $Df(a)$ invertible. Then: (1) $\exists$ open $U\ni a$, $W\ni f(a)$ s.t. $f|_U$ is 1-1 and $f(U)=W$; (2) $f^{-1}\in C^1$ on $W$; (3) $Df^{-1}(f(x))=[Df(x)]^{-1}$ $\forall x\in U$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Inverse FT):} $f(x)=x^3+x-1$, $f'(x)=3x^2+1>0$, strictly increasing, $C^1$, $Df(x)\neq0$. $f(0)=-1$, $f(1)=1$, so by continuity $\exists$ unique $C^1$ inverse on $[f(0),f(1)]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Implicit Function Theorem (11.47):} $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}$ open, $F\in C^1$, $F(a,b)=0$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$. If $\det\frac{\partial(F_1,\dots,F_n)}{\partial(x_1,\dots,x_n)}(a,b)\neq0$, then: (1) $\exists$ open $W\subset\mathbb R^p$ with $b\in W$; (2) $\exists$ unique $C^1$ function $g:W\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(b)=a$ and $F(g(t),t)=0$ $\forall t\in W$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Implicit FT):} $F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1$. At $(a,b)=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$, $\partial F/\partial x=2x\neq0$, so locally $y=g(x)$ solves $x^2+g(x)^2=1$. Indeed $g(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ near this point.\smallskip

\textbf{Lagrange Multipliers (11.63):} $f\in C^1$, constraint $g(x)=0$ where $g\in C^1$. At local extremum of $f$ on $\{g=0\}$: $\nabla f(a)=\lambda\nabla g(a)$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.\smallskip

\textbf{Second Derivative Test, 2 vars (11.59):} $f\in C^2$, $\nabla f(a)=0$. Let $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$. If $D>0$: $f_{xx}>0\implies$ local min; $f_{xx}<0\implies$ local max. If $D<0$: saddle point. If $D=0$: inconclusive.\smallskip

\section*{Lebesgue Integration (Tao Ch8)}
\textbf{Simple Functions (8.1):} $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ simple if $f(\Omega)$ finite. Every simple $f=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\chi_{E_j}$ with $E_j$ disjoint, measurable. $\chi_E$ is characteristic/indicator function.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral of Simple (8.1.6):} $f\ge0$ simple: $\int_\Omega f:=\sum_{\lambda\in f(\Omega),\lambda>0}\lambda\,m(\{x\in\Omega:f(x)=\lambda\})$. Equivalently $\int_\Omega\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}=\sum c_j m(E_j)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Basic Properties (8.1.10):} $0\le\int f\le\infty$; $\int f=0\iff f=0$ a.e.; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $\int cf=c\int f$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral of Non-neg Functions (8.2.2):} $f:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ measurable: $\int_\Omega f:=\sup\{\int_\Omega s:0\le s\le f,\ s\text{ simple}\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{MCT (8.2.9):} $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, $f_n\uparrow f$ a.e. $\implies\int f_n\uparrow\int f$. (Key: can interchange limit and integral for monotone seq.)\smallskip

\textbf{Fatou (8.2.13):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable $\implies\int\liminf f_k\le\liminf\int f_k$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1)}$, $\liminf f_n=0$, $\int\liminf=0$, $\liminf\int f_n=1$, strict inequality.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli (8.2.15):} $\sum m(E_k)<\infty\implies$ a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $E_k$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Integrable (8.3.1):} $f$ measurable, $\int_\Omega|f|<\infty$. Write $f=f^+-f^-$, $|f|=f^++f^-$. $\int_\Omega f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$. $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\textbf{DCT (8.3.4):} $f_n\to f$ a.e., $|f_n|\le F$ with $F\in L^1$ $\implies\int f_n\to\int f$ and $f\in L^1$. (Most commonly used theorem.)\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (DCT):} $f_n(x)=n\chi_{[0,1/n]}(x)$, $f_n\to0$ a.e., $|f_n|\le1\in L^1$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Properties (8.3.3):} $f,g\in L^1$: $\int cf=c\int f$; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$; $f=g$ a.e. $\implies\int f=\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e. (8.2.14):} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e.\smallskip

\textbf{Fubini (8.5.1):} $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ abs integrable. Then for a.e. $x$, $f(x,y)$ abs integrable in $y$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^2}f=\int_{\mathbb R}(\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)dy)dx=\int_{\mathbb R}(\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)dx)dy$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Fubini):} $\int_{[0,1]^2}xy\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1(\int_0^1 xy\,dy)dx=\int_0^1(x/2)dx=1/4$. Since $xy\ge0$, Fubini applies directly.\smallskip

\textbf{Riemann $\Rightarrow$ Lebesgue (8.4.1):} $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e., and $\int_{\text{Riem}}f=\int_{\text{Leb}}f$. \textbf{Ex:} Dirichlet's function $f=1_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$: not Riemann integrable but Lebesgue integrable with $\int f=0$.\smallskip

\section*{Lebesgue Measure (Tao Ch7)}
\textbf{Outer Measure $m^*$ (7.2.4):} $m^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum|I_j|:\cup I_j\supset E,\ \{I_j\}\text{ countable open intervals}\right\}$. $m^*$ is defined for every set.\smallskip

\textbf{Measurable (Carathéodory, 7.4.1):} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ Lebesgue measurable $\iff$ $m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ $\forall A\subset\mathbb R^n$. Equivalently: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ open $U\supset E$ with $m^*(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Measure $m$:} $m(E)=m^*(E)$ for all measurable $E$. All open sets, closed sets, intervals, Borel sets are measurable. $\mathbb Q$, countable sets, null sets are measurable with $m(E)=0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$E\subset\mathbb R^n$ has measure zero: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ countable cover $\{I_j\}$ with $\sum|I_j|<\varepsilon$. Almost everywhere (a.e.): property holds except on a measure zero set. $f$ Lebesgue measurable: $\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $\{f>\alpha\}$ is measurable (equivalently $f^{-1}(B)$ measurable $\forall$ open box $B$).\smallskip

\textbf{Null Sets (7.4.4f):} Every countable set has measure zero. Finite/countable union of null sets is null. $m(E)=0\implies E$ is measurable. \textbf{Ex:} If $m^*(E)=0$, for any $A$, subadditivity gives $m^*(A)\le m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)\le0+m^*(A\setminus E)\le m^*(A)$, so Carathéodory holds.\smallskip

\textbf{Properties of Measurable Sets (7.4.4):} $\sigma$-algebra: $E$ meas. $\implies$ $E^c$ meas.; countable unions/intersections of meas. sets are meas. (hence all Borel sets are meas.). $m(\varnothing)=0$, $m((a,b))=b-a$. Finite/countable additivity. Translation invariance: $m(E+x)=m(E)$. Continuity from below/above: $E_k\uparrow E$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\uparrow m(E)$; $E_k\downarrow E$, $m(E_1)<\infty$ $\implies$ $m(E_k)\downarrow m(E)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties (7.2.5):} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$. \textbf{Ex:} $m^*(\mathbb Q)=0$: enumerate $\mathbb Q=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$, cover $q_k$ by interval of length $\varepsilon/2^k$, so $m^*(\mathbb Q)\le\varepsilon$. $m^*([0,1])=1$.\smallskip

\textbf{Existence of Lebesgue Measure (7.1.1):} There exists a concept of measurable set and $m(E)$ obeying: (i) Borel: all open/closed sets measurable; (ii) complement; (iii) countable unions/intersections; (iv) positivity; (v) monotonicity; (vi) finite/countable additivity; (vii) normalization $m([0,1]^n)=1$; (viii) translation invariance. Lebesgue measure is unique.\smallskip

\textbf{Non-measurable sets (7.3):} Outer measure is not finitely additive. Vitali set: using axiom of choice, partition $\mathbb R$ into cosets of $\mathbb Q$, pick one representative from each coset in $[0,1]$. This set is not Lebesgue measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity/Measurability of Functions (7.5.2,7.5.5):} Continuous functions are measurable. $f$ measurable, $g$ continuous $\implies$ $g\circ f$ measurable. $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ measurable $\iff$ each $f_j$ measurable. $f$ measurable $\iff$ $f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ measurable $\forall a$ (7.5.8).\smallskip

\textbf{Almost everywhere modification (7.5.5 ex):} $f$ Lebesgue measurable, $g=f$ a.e. $\implies$ $g$ is Lebesgue measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Limits of Measurable Functions (7.5.10):} If $f_k$ are measurable, then $\sup f_k$, $\inf f_k$, $\limsup f_k$, $\liminf f_k$ are measurable. Pointwise limit of measurable functions is measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{$L^p$ Spaces:} $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. H\"older: $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Minkowski: $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\smallskip

\end{multicols}

It's in **Ch8** (Euclidean Spaces), from **Definition 8.28** of the textbook:

**Connected**: A set $E$ cannot be separated into two nonempty disjoint relatively-open sets. Formally, $E$ is connected iff there do not exist nonempty disjoint relatively open sets $U, V \subset E$ such that $E = U \cup V$. Equivalently, $E$ is connected iff the only subsets of $E$ that are both relatively open and relatively closed in $E$ are $\varnothing$ and $E$ itself.

Equivalently in $\mathbb R$: $E \subset \mathbb R$ is connected $\iff$ $E$ is an **interval** (Theorem 8.30). Rectangles in $\mathbb R^n$ are connected.

\documentclass[8pt]{extarticle}
\usepackage[margin=0.15in, landscape, top=0.12in, bottom=0.12in, left=0.12in, right=0.12in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath, amssymb, enumitem}

\begin{document}

\fontsize{6pt}{7.5pt}\selectfont

\begin{multicols}{3}

\section*{Ch6. Infinite Series of Real Numbers}
\textbf{Defs:} $s_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k$. $\sum a_k$ converges to $s$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|s_n-s|<\varepsilon$. Diverges: $\{s_n\}$ has no limit. Abs conv: $\sum|a_k|<\infty$. Conditional: conv but not abs.\smallskip

\textbf{Divergence Test (6.5):} $a_k\not\to0\implies\sum a_k$ diverges. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum\sin k$: $a_k=\sin k\not\to0$, diverges.\smallskip

\textbf{Geometric (6.7):} $\sum_{k=0}^\infty x^k=\frac1{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$, diverges for $|x|\ge1$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum(1/2)^k=1$, $\sum(-1)^k$ diverges.\smallskip

\textbf{Cauchy Criterion (6.8):} $\sum a_k$ conv $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:m\ge n\ge N\implies\sum_{k=n}^m a_k<\varepsilon$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum(-1)^k/k$ satisfies Cauchy, converges (conditionally).\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Test (6.12):} $f\ge0$ decr on $[1,\infty)$. $\sum f(k)$ conv $\iff\int_1^\infty f<\infty$. $\sum1/k^p$ conv $\iff p>1$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum1/k\log k$ diverges. $\sum1/(k\log^2k)$ conv.\smallskip

\textbf{Comparison (6.14):} $0\le a_k\le b_k$ for large $k$: $\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$; $\sum a_k=\infty\implies\sum b_k=\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{LCT (6.16):} $L=\lim a_k/b_k$, $b_k>0$. $0<L<\infty$: same conv. $L=0$+$\sum b_k<\infty\implies\sum a_k<\infty$. $L=\infty$+$\sum b_k=\infty\implies\sum a_k=\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Conv (6.20):} Abs conv $\implies$conv (converse false). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Root Test (6.23):} $r=\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Ratio Test (6.24):} $r=\lim|a_{k+1}/a_k|$. $r<1\implies$abs conv; $r>1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $\sum k/e^k$ conv ($r=1/e<1$). $\sum k^2/(k+1)$ diverges. $\sum1/k^2$ conv ($p=2>1$). $\sum(-1)^k/k$ cond conv.\smallskip

\textbf{Rearrangements (6.27):} If $\sum a_k$ abs conv, every rearrangement $\to$ same sum. Cond conv $\implies$ can rearrange to any $x\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abel's Formula (6.30):} $A_{n,m}=\sum_{k=m}^n a_k$. $\sum_{k=m}^n a_kb_k=A_{n,m}b_n-\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}A_{k,m}(b_{k+1}-b_k)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test (6.31):} $\sum a_k$ partial sums bounded + $b_k\downarrow0$ $\implies\sum a_kb_k$ converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Alt Series Test (6.32):} $a_k\downarrow0\implies\sum(-1)^ka_k$ converges.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Test Error (6.35):} $0\le\sum_{k=1}^n f(k)-\int_1^n f\le f(1)$. If $\sum f(k)$ conv: $0\le s-s_n+\int_n^\infty f\le f(n)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Alt Series Error (6.38):} $a_k\downarrow0$, $s=\sum(-1)^ka_k$, $|s-s_n|\le a_{n+1}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Logarithmic Test (6.42):} $p=\lim\frac{\log(1/|a_k|)}{\log k}$. $p>1\implies$abs conv; $p<1\implies$diverge.\smallskip

\textbf{Raabe's Test (6.43):} $|a_{k+1}/a_k|\le1-p/k+O(1/k)$ with $p>1\implies\sum a_k$ abs conv.\smallskip

\section*{Ch7. Infinite Series of Functions}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f_n\to f$ ptwise: $\forall x\in E$, $\lim f_n(x)=f(x)$. $f_n\to f$ uniformly: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$ ($N$ depends only on $\varepsilon$). Radius of conv $R$: abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (7.9):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ cont at $x_0\in E$ $\implies f$ cont at $x_0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Integrability (7.10):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$, each integrable $\implies f$ integrable and $\int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n/n$ on $[0,1]$, uniform conv since $|x^n/n|\le1/n\to0$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Cauchy Criterion (7.11):} $f_n$ conv uniformly on $E$ $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n,m\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Differentiability (7.12):} (1) $(a,b)$ bounded; (2) each $f_n$ diff on $(a,b)$; (3) $f_n(x_0)\to L$ for some $x_0$; (4) $f_n'$ converges uniformly on $(a,b)$ $\implies$ $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $(a,b)$ and $f'=\lim f_n'$.\smallskip

\textbf{Term-by-Term Diff (7.14):} (1) $I$ open interval; (2) each $f_k$ differentiable on $I$; (3) $\sum f_k$ converges at some $x_0\in I$; (4) $\sum f_k'$ converges uniformly on $I$ $\implies$ $(\sum f_k)'=\sum f_k'$ on $I$.\smallskip

\textbf{Weierstrass M-Test (7.15):} $|f_k(x)|\le M_k$ for $x\in E$, $\sum M_k<\infty\implies\sum f_k$ abs conv and uniformly on $E$. \textbf{Ex:} $\sum x^k/k$ on $[0,r]$, $r<1$: $\sum r^k/k<\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Dirichlet's Test for Uniform Conv (7.16):} $|\sum_{k=1}^n f_k(x)|\le M$ for all $n,x\in E$ and $g_k\downarrow0$ uniformly $\implies\sum f_kg_k$ converges uniformly.\smallskip

\textbf{Power Series Radius (7.21):} $S(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$, $R=1/\limsup|a_k|^{1/k}$. $S$ abs conv for $|x-x_0|<R$, uniformly on any $[a,b]\subset(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$.\smallskip

\textbf{PS Diff \& Int (7.26,7.32):} On $(x_0-R,x_0+R)$, $S\in C^\infty$ and $S'(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty k a_k(x-x_0)^{k-1}$, $\int S=\sum\frac{a_k}{k+1}(x-x_0)^{k+1}+C$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abel's Theorem (7.27):} If $\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ converges on $[a,b]$, then it converges uniformly on $[a,b]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniqueness (7.39):} If $f(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ on open interval $I$, then $a_k=f^{(k)}(x_0)/k!$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$: ptwise $f_n\to0$ for $x<1$, $f_n(1)=1$, not continuous at $x=1$ (non-uniform). $f_n(x)=x^n(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$: uniform conv by M-test ($x^n(1-x)\le 1$).\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (proving non-uniform):} To show $f_n(x)=1/(nx)\to0$ not uniform on $(0,1)$: negation says $\exists\varepsilon>0$ s.t. $\forall N$, $\exists n\ge N$, $\exists x\in(0,1)$ with $|1/(nx)-0|\ge\varepsilon$. Take $\varepsilon=1$, pick $x=1/n$, then $|1/(n\cdot1/n)|=1\ge1$. QED.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Boundedness + Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} $f_n$ uniformly bounded on $E$ + $f_n\to f$ uniformly $\implies f$ bounded on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Product of Uniformly Conv Functions:} If $f_n\to f$, $g_n\to g$ uniformly on $E$ and $f,g$ bounded on $E$, then $f_ng_n\to fg$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cesàro Mean:} If $b_k\to b$, then $\frac{b_1+\dots+b_n}{n}\to b$. Equivalently, Stolz-Cesàro: if $c_n\to c$ and $a_n$ monotone or $d_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\to\infty$, then $\lim\frac{a_n}{d_n}=L\implies\lim\frac{\sum a_k}{\sum d_k}=L$.\smallskip

\textbf{Arith. Mean Conv:} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ bounded $\implies$ $\frac{f_1+\dots+f_n}{n}\to f$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\section*{Ch8. Euclidean Spaces $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent Open ball: $B_r(a)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x-a\|<r\}$. Closed ball: $\{\|x-a\|\le r\}$. $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ is \textbf{open}: $\forall a\in V$, $\exists\varepsilon>0:B_\varepsilon(a)\subset V$. $E$ is \textbf{closed}: $E^c$ is open. \textbf{Relatively open in} $A$: $E=A\cap V$ for some open $V$. \textbf{Relatively closed in} $A$: $E=A\cap F$ for some closed $F$. \textbf{Compact}: every open cover has a finite subcover. \textbf{Connected}: cannot be separated into two nonempty disjoint relatively-open sets. \textbf{Interior} $E^\circ$: largest open set $\subset E$. \textbf{Closure} $\overline{E}$: smallest closed set $\supset E$. \textbf{Boundary} $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$. \textbf{Limit point}: $x$ is limit point of $E$ if every $B_\varepsilon(x)$ contains $y\in E$ with $y\ne x$. \textbf{Dense}: $\overline{E}=\mathbb R^n$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cauchy-Schwarz (8.5):} $|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, equality $\iff x,y$ parallel or one is zero.\smallskip

\textbf{Triangle Inequalities (8.6):} $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$, $\|x-y\|\ge|\|x\|-\|y\||$.\smallskip

\textbf{Norm Inequalities (8.7):} $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$, $\|x\|\le\|x\|_1\le\sqrt n\|x\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Cross Product (8.9):} $x,y\in\mathbb R^3$: $x\times y\perp x$ and $x\times y\perp y$. $\|x\times y\|=\|x\|\|y\|\sin\theta$. $x\times(y\times z)=(x\cdot z)y-(x\cdot y)z$.\smallskip

\textbf{Linear Maps (8.15-8.18):} $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ linear $\iff$ $T(x)=Bx$ for unique $m\times n$ matrix $B$. Operator norm: $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\neq0}\frac{\|T(x)\|}{\|x\|}$, and $\|T(x)\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Balls are Open/Closed (8.21):} Open ball $B_r(a)$ is open; closed ball $\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is closed. Shell $\{x:s\le\|x-a\|\le r\}$ is neither open nor closed.\smallskip

\textbf{Open/Closed Properties (8.24):} Arbitrary unions of open are open; finite intersections of open are open. Arbitrary intersections of closed are closed; finite unions of closed are closed.\smallskip

\textbf{Relatively Open/Closed (8.26):} If $C\subset E\subset\mathbb R^n$: (1) $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ relatively open in $E$. (2) $C$ relatively open in $E$ + $E$ open in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $C$ open in $\mathbb R^n$.\smallskip

\textbf{Connected $\iff$ Interval (8.30):} $E\subset\mathbb R$ connected $\iff$ $E$ is an interval. Rectangles in $\mathbb R^n$ are connected.\smallskip

\textbf{Interior, Closure, Boundary (8.31,8.34):} Interior $E^\circ$ is largest open $\subset E$; closure $\overline{E}$ is smallest closed $\supset E$; boundary $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$.\smallskip

\textbf{Boundary Thm (8.36):} $\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus E^\circ$. Also $\overline{E}=E^\circ\cup\partial E$, disjoint.\smallskip

\textbf{Closure/Interior Monotonicity (8.37):} $A\subset B$ $\implies$ $\overline{A}\subset\overline{B}$ and $A^\circ\subset B^\circ$.\smallskip

\textbf{Distance Between Sets (8.33):} $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{\|x-y\|:x\in A,y\in B\}$. If $A,B$ are compact and disjoint, then $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex:} $\mathbb Q$ is dense in $\mathbb R$. $(0,1)$ is open, not closed. $[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q$ is not closed, not open. Cantor set is perfect and nowhere dense.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (proving open/closed):} To show $V=\{x:s<\|x-a\|<r\}$ is open: for any $y\in V$, set $\varepsilon=\min\{s-\|y-a\|,\|y-a\|-r\}>0$. Then $B_\varepsilon(y)\subset V$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (counterexamples):} $(A\cup B)^\circ\neq A^\circ\cup B^\circ$: $A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$, then $(A\cup B)^\circ=(0,2)$ but $A^\circ\cup B^\circ=(0,1)\cup(1,2)$. $\overline{A\cap B}\neq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$: $A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$, then $\overline{A\cap B}=\varnothing$ but $\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}=\{1\}$.\smallskip

\section*{Ch9. Convergence in $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\dots,x_k^{(n)})\to a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\iff x_k^{(j)}\to a_j$ for each $j$. Bounded: $\exists M>0:\|x_k\|\le M\ \forall k$. Cauchy: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:k,m\ge N\implies\|x_k-x_m\|<\varepsilon$. $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to a$: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists\delta>0:0<\|x-a\|<\delta\implies\|f(x)-L\|<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Conv $\iff$ Componentwise (9.2):} $x_k^{(j)}\to a_j\ \forall j\iff x_k\to a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Sequence Properties (9.4,9.6):} Uniqueness. Subseq $\to$ same limit. Conv $\implies$ bounded. Conv $\iff$ Cauchy.\smallskip

\textbf{Bolzano-Weierstrass (9.5):} Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb R^n$ has a convergent subsequence. \textbf{Ex:} $x_k=(\sin k,\cos k)$ bounded in $\mathbb R^2$, has conv subseq.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit Point Char (9.7):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $E$ contains all its limit points.\smallskip

\textbf{Closed $\iff$ Sequential (9.8):} $E$ closed $\iff$ $x_k\in E$, $x_k\to x$ $\implies x\in E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel Covering (9.9):} Every open cover of a compact set has a finite subcover.\smallskip

\textbf{Compact + Isolated Points $\implies$ Finite (9.12):} $K$ compact, each $x\in K$ isolated ($\exists r>0:B_r(x)\cap K=\{x\}$) $\implies$ $K$ is finite.\smallskip

\textbf{Limit Laws (9.15):} $\lim(f+g)=L+M$, $\lim(\alpha f)=\alpha L$, $\lim(f\cdot g)=L\cdot M$. Squeeze: $g\le h\le f$, $\lim f=\lim g=L\implies\lim h=L$. Composition: $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L$, $\lim_{y\to L}h(y)=M\implies\lim_{x\to a}h(g(x))=M$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Continuity $\iff$ Coord-wise (9.18):} $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m):E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous at $a$ $\iff$ each $f_j$ is continuous at $a$.\smallskip

\textbf{$\mathbb R^n$ Dot Product Conv (9.22):} $x_k\to0$ in $\mathbb R^n$, $y_k$ bounded in $\mathbb R^n$ $\implies$ $x_k\cdot y_k\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Continuity on Compact (9.25):} $E$ compact, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f$ uniformly continuous.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous $\iff$ Preimage of Open (9.26):} $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\iff$ $f^{-1}(V)$ relatively open in $E$ for every open $V\subset\mathbb R^m$.\smallskip

\textbf{Compact $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (9.29):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous on $K$ $\implies f(K)$ compact. Hence $f$ bounded and attains max/min (Extreme Value Thm 9.32).\smallskip

\textbf{Continuity $\Rightarrow$ Connectedness (9.30):} $E$ connected, $f:E\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous $\implies f(E)$ is connected.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous Inverse (9.33):} $K$ compact, $f:K\to\mathbb R^m$ is 1-1 and continuous $\implies f^{-1}$ continuous on $f(K)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Heine-Borel (9.11):} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ compact $\iff$ $E$ is closed and bounded.\smallskip

\textbf{Dini's Theorem (9.40):} $K$ compact, $f_k:K\to\mathbb R$ ptwise monotone to continuous $f$ $\implies f_k\to f$ uniformly on $K$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (proving no limit):} To show $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ DNE: along $y=x$ gives $1/2$, along $y=0$ gives $0$. Since $1/2\neq0$, limit DNE.\smallskip

\section*{Ch11. Differentiability on $\mathbb R^n$}
\textbf{Defs (11.1,11.12):}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$f:V\to\mathbb R^m$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open. $f$ diff at $a\in V$ $\iff$ $\exists$ linear $Df(a):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ s.t. $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Df(a)h\|}{\|h\|}=0$. $Df(a)$ = Jacobian. If $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$, then $Df=(J_{ij})$, $J_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$. $f\in C^p$: all partials of order $\le p$ exist and are continuous.\smallskip

\textbf{Equality of Mixed Partials (11.2):} If $f\in C^1$, and one mixed partial $f_{xy}$ or $f_{yx}$ exists and is continuous at $(a,b)$, then $f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b)$. In particular, if $f\in C^2$, then $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$.\smallskip

\textbf{Differentiability $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (11.13):} $f$ diff at $a$ $\implies$ all partials exist and $f$ continuous at $a$. But partials exist $\not\Rightarrow$ diff.\smallskip

\textbf{Continuous Partials $\Rightarrow$ Diff (11.15):} If all $\partial f/\partial x_j$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of $a$, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (not diff):} $f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$, $f(0,0)=0$. $f_x(0,0)=0$, $f_y(0,0)=0$, but not diff at $(0,0)$. With $h=(t,t)$, ratio $=1/2\not\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Derivative Rules (11.20):} Sum, scalar multiple, product, quotient rules all hold for the total derivative $D$. $(Df\cdot Dg)(x)=Df(x)\cdot Dg(x)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Tangent Hyperplane (11.21):} If $f:V\to\mathbb R$ diff at $a$, the tangent hyperplane is $y=f(a)+Df(a)(x-a)$. The surface is differentiable at $a$ iff the graph has a tangent hyperplane.\smallskip

\textbf{Chain Rule (11.28):} $D(f\circ g)(a)=Df(g(a))Dg(a)$. Scalar: $\partial f/\partial x_i=\sum_j\frac{\partial f}{\partial u_j}\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}$. \textbf{Ex:} $f(u)=e^u$, $u=g(x)=x^2$, $(f\circ g)'=e^{x^2}\cdot2x$.\smallskip

\textbf{Mean Value Inequality (11.30):} $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, connected; $f:U\to\mathbb R$ diff; $\|Df(x)\|\le M$ $\forall x\in U$ $\implies$ $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|$ $\forall x,y\in U$.\smallskip

\textbf{Convex MVT (11.32):} $U$ convex, $f:U\to\mathbb R^m$ diff: $\exists c\in U$ with $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le\|Df(c)\|\|x-y\|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Taylor's Theorem (11.37):} $f\in C^{k+1}$: $f(b)=f(a)+\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{j!}(D^jf(a))(b-a)^j+\frac1{(k+1)!}(D^{k+1}f(c))(b-a)^{k+1}$ for some $c$ on $[a,b]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Taylor 2nd Order, 2 vars (11.59):} $f(a+h,b+k)=f(a,b)+hf_x+kf_y+\frac12(h^2f_{xx}+2hkf_{xy}+k^2f_{yy})+o(h^2+k^2)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Inverse Function Theorem (11.41):} $f:V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ open, $f\in C^1$, $a\in V$, $Df(a)$ invertible. Then: (1) $\exists$ open $U\ni a$, $W\ni f(a)$ s.t. $f|_U$ is 1-1 and $f(U)=W$; (2) $f^{-1}\in C^1$ on $W$; (3) $Df^{-1}(f(x))=[Df(x)]^{-1}$ $\forall x\in U$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Inverse FT):} $f(x)=x^3+x-1$, $f'(x)=3x^2+1>0$, strictly increasing, $C^1$, $Df(x)\neq0$. $f(0)=-1$, $f(1)=1$, so $\exists$ unique $C^1$ inverse on $[f(0),f(1)]$.\smallskip

\textbf{Implicit Function Theorem (11.47):} $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):V\to\mathbb R^n$, $V\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}$ open, $F\in C^1$, $F(a,b)=0$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $b\in\mathbb R^p$. If $\det\frac{\partial(F_1,\dots,F_n)}{\partial(x_1,\dots,x_n)}(a,b)\neq0$, then: (1) $\exists$ open $W\subset\mathbb R^p$ with $b\in W$; (2) $\exists$ unique $C^1$ function $g:W\to\mathbb R^n$ with $g(b)=a$ and $F(g(t),t)=0$ $\forall t\in W$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Implicit FT):} $F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1$. At $(a,b)=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$, $\partial F/\partial x=2x\neq0$, so locally $y=g(x)$ solves $x^2+g(x)^2=1$. Indeed $g(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ near this point.\smallskip

\textbf{Lagrange Multipliers (11.63):} $f\in C^1$, constraint $g(x)=0$ where $g\in C^1$. At local extremum of $f$ on $\{g=0\}$: $\nabla f(a)=\lambda\nabla g(a)$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.\smallskip

\textbf{Second Derivative Test, 2 vars (11.59):} $f\in C^2$, $\nabla f(a)=0$. Let $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$. If $D>0$: $f_{xx}>0\implies$ local min; $f_{xx}<0\implies$ local max. If $D<0$: saddle point. If $D=0$: inconclusive.\smallskip

\section*{Lebesgue Integration (Tao Ch8)}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent Simple function: $f(\Omega)$ finite. Every simple $f=\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}$ with $E_j$ disjoint, measurable. $\chi_E$ is characteristic/indicator function. $f\ge0$ measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral of Simple (8.1.6):} $f\ge0$ simple: $\int_\Omega f:=\sum_{\lambda\in f(\Omega),\lambda>0}\lambda\,m(\{x:f(x)=\lambda\})$. Equivalently $\int_\Omega\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}=\sum c_j m(E_j)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Basic Properties (8.1.10):} $0\le\int f\le\infty$; $\int f=0\iff f=0$ a.e.; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $\int cf=c\int f$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral of Non-neg Functions (8.2.2):} $f:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ measurable: $\int_\Omega f:=\sup\{\int_\Omega s:0\le s\le f,\ s\text{ simple}\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{MCT (8.2.9):} $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, $f_n\uparrow f$ a.e. $\implies\int f_n\uparrow\int f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Fatou (8.2.13):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable $\implies\int\liminf f_k\le\liminf\int f_k$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1)}$, $\liminf f_n=0$, $\int\liminf=0$, $\liminf\int f_n=1$, strict inequality.\smallskip

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e. (8.2.14):} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli (8.2.15):} $\sum m(E_k)<\infty\implies$ a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $E_k$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Integrable (8.3.1):} $f$ measurable, $\int_\Omega|f|<\infty$. Write $f=f^+-f^-$, $|f|=f^++f^-$. $\int_\Omega f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$. $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\nobreak\smallskip\noindent Simple function: $f(\Omega)$ finite. Every simple $f=\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}$ with $E_j$ disjoint, measurable. $\chi_E$ is characteristic/indicator function. $f\ge0$ measurable.\smallskip

\textbf{Lebesgue Integral of Simple (8.1.6):} $f\ge0$ simple: $\int_\Omega f:=\sum_{\lambda\in f(\Omega),\lambda>0}\lambda\,m(\{x:f(x)=\lambda\})$. Equivalently $\int_\Omega\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}=\sum c_j m(E_j)$.\smallskip

\textbf{Basic Properties (8.1.10):} $0\le\int f\le\infty$; $\int f=0\iff f=0$ a.e.; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $\int cf=c\int f$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral of Non-neg Functions (8.2.2):} $f:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ measurable: $\int_\Omega f:=\sup\{\int_\Omega s:0\le s\le f,\ s\text{ simple}\}$.\smallskip

\textbf{MCT (8.2.9):} $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, $f_n\uparrow f$ a.e. $\implies\int f_n\uparrow\int f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Fatou (8.2.13):} $f_k\ge0$ measurable $\implies\int\liminf f_k\le\liminf\int f_k$. \textbf{Ex:} $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1)}$, $\liminf f_n=0$, $\int\liminf=0$, $\liminf\int f_n=1$, strict inequality.\smallskip

\textbf{Finite $f$ a.e. (8.2.14):} $f\ge0$ measurable, $\int f<\infty$ $\implies$ $f<\infty$ a.e.\smallskip

\textbf{Borel-Cantelli (8.2.15):} $\sum m(E_k)<\infty\implies$ a.e. $x$ belongs to only finitely many $E_k$.\smallskip

\textbf{Abs Integrable (8.3.1):} $f$ measurable, $\int_\Omega|f|<\infty$. Write $f=f^+-f^-$, $|f|=f^++f^-$. $\int_\Omega f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$. $|\int f|\le\int|f|$.\smallskip

\textbf{Integral Properties (8.3.3):} $f,g\in L^1$: $\int cf=c\int f$; $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$; $f\le g\implies\int f\le\int g$; $f=g$ a.e. $\implies\int f=\int g$.\smallskip

\textbf{DCT (8.3.4):} $f_n\to f$ a.e., $|f_n|\le F$ with $F\in L^1$ $\implies\int f_n\to\int f$ and $f\in L^1$. (Most commonly used.)\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (DCT):} $f_n(x)=n\chi_{[0,1/n]}(x)$, $f_n\to0$ a.e., $|f_n|\le1\in L^1$, so $\int_0^1 f_n\to0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Fubini (8.5.1):} $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ abs integrable. Then for a.e. $x$, $f(x,y)$ abs integrable in $y$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^2}f=\int_{\mathbb R}(\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)dy)dx=\int_{\mathbb R}(\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)dx)dy$.\smallskip

\textbf{Ex (Fubini):} $\int_{[0,1]^2}xy\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1(\int_0^1 xy\,dy)dx=\int_0^1(x/2)dx=1/4$. Since $xy\ge0$, Fubini applies directly.\smallskip

\textbf{Riemann $\Rightarrow$ Lebesgue (8.4.1):} $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ Riemann integrable $\iff$ $f$ is continuous a.e., and $\int_{\text{Riem}}f=\int_{\text{Leb}}f$. \textbf{Ex:} Dirichlet's function $f=1_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$: not Riemann integrable but Lebesgue integrable with $\int f=0$.\smallskip

\section*{$L^p$ Spaces}
\textbf{Defs:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent$\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$, $1\le p<\infty$. $f\in L^p$ means $\|f\|_p<\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{H\"older:} $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$.\smallskip

\textbf{Minkowski:} $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$.\smallskip

\textbf{Outer Measure $m^*$ (7.2.4):} $m^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum|I_j|:\cup I_j\supset E,\ \{I_j\}\text{ countable open intervals}\right\}$. $m^*$ is defined for every set.\smallskip

\textbf{Outer Measure Properties (7.2.5):} $A\subset B\implies m^*(A)\le m^*(B)$. Countable subadditivity: $m^*(\cup A_k)\le\sum m^*(A_k)$. \textbf{Ex:} $m^*(\mathbb Q)=0$: enumerate $\mathbb Q=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$, cover $q_k$ by interval of length $\varepsilon/2^k$, so $m^*(\mathbb Q)\le\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Measurable (Carathéodory, 7.4.1):} $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ Lebesgue measurable $\iff$ $m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ $\forall A\subset\mathbb R^n$. Equivalently: $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists$ open $U\supset E$ with $m^*(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.\smallskip

\textbf{Null Sets (7.4.4f):} Every countable set has measure zero. Finite/countable union of null sets is null. $m(E)=0\implies E$ is measurable.\smallskip

Lebesgue measure is unique.\smallskip

\textbf{Defs:}\par

**What outer measure $m^*$ DOES satisfy** (the "good" properties):
- (v) $m^*(\varnothing) = 0$

**Countable sub-additivity** of outer measure (property x in the cheatsheet).

Since $A \cap (0, \infty)$ and $A \setminus (0, \infty)$ are disjoint and their union is $A$:

$$m^*(A) = m^*\!\bigl((A \cap (0,\infty)) \cup (A \setminus (0,\infty))\bigr) \leq m^*(A \cap (0,\infty)) + m^*(A \setminus (0,\infty))$$

That's exactly the sub-additivity inequality: the measure of a union is at most the sum of the measures. It works for any countable family of sets, so a finite (or just two) disjoint sets is a special case.

\begin{center} \Large Homework 6 Solutions -- Math 3033
\end{center}
\medskip

\textbf{P1-2.} Let $\{A_j\}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets ($A_j \subseteq A_{j+1}$).

\medskip
\noindent(a) \emph{Continuity from below:} Define $B_1 = A_1$, and for $j \geq 2$ set $B_j = A_j \setminus A_{j-1}$. Then the $B_j$ are disjoint and measurable, and $\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j = \bigsqcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j$ (a disjoint union). By countable additivity,
\[m\!\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j\right)=m\!\left(\bigsqcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j\right)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty m(B_j).\]
Since $m(A_j) = \sum_{k=1}^j m(B_k)$, taking the limit gives $\lim_{j\to\infty} m(A_j) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty m(B_j) = m(\bigcup A_j)$.

\medskip
\noindent(b) \emph{Continuity from above (with finite initial set):} Since $m(A_1) < \infty$, the sets $C_j = A_1 \setminus A_j$ form an increasing sequence of measurable sets. By part (a),
\[m\!\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty C_j\right)=\lim_{j\to\infty} m(C_j).\]
But $\bigcup_j C_j = A_1 \setminus \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty A_j$ and $m(C_j) = m(A_1) - m(A_j)$. Hence
\[m(A_1)-m\!\left(\bigcap_{j=1}^\infty A_j\right)=\lim_{j\to\infty}\bigl(m(A_1)-m(A_j)\bigr),\]
so $m(\bigcap_j A_j) = \lim_{j\to\infty} m(A_j)$.

\medskip

\textbf{P3.} Let $f: \Omega \to [0,\infty]$ be measurable with $\int_\Omega f < \infty$. Define $E_k = \{x \in \Omega: f(x) > k\}$ for each $k \in \N$. Then $E_k$ is measurable (since $f$ is measurable) and $E_k \downarrow \varnothing$ as $k \to \infty$ on the set $\{f < \infty\}$. Let $E = \{x: f(x) = \infty\}$. For any $x \in E$, $f(x) > k$ for all $k$, so $x \in E_k$ for all $k$. Thus $E \subseteq \bigcap_{k=1}^\infty E_k$.

Now, $k \cdot \chi_{E_k} \leq f \cdot \chi_{E_k} \leq f$, so integrating gives $k \cdot m(E_k) \leq \int_{E_k} f \leq \int_\Omega f < \infty$. Hence $m(E_k) \leq \frac{1}{k} \int_\Omega f$. Since $E \subseteq E_k$ for every $k$, we have $m(E) \leq m(E_k) \leq \frac{1}{k} \int_\Omega f$ for all $k$, so $m(E) = 0$.

\medskip

\textbf{P4.} (Borel--Cantelli Lemma) Let $\Omega_n$ be measurable with $\sum_{n=1}^\infty m(\Omega_n) < \infty$. Let
\[E = \left\{x \in \R^n : x \in \Omega_n \text{ for infinitely many } n\right\} = \bigcap_{N=1}^\infty \bigcup_{n=N}^\infty \Omega_n.\]
For each $N$, by countable sub-additivity,
\[m\!\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^\infty \Omega_n\right) \leq \sum_{n=N}^\infty m(\Omega_n).\]
Since $\sum_{n=1}^\infty m(\Omega_n) < \infty$, the tail sum $\sum_{n=N}^\infty m(\Omega_n) \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. Thus $m(\bigcup_{n=N}^\infty \Omega_n) \to 0$. The sets $\bigcup_{n=N}^\infty \Omega_n$ decrease with $N$, and $m$ is continuous from above (since $m(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \Omega_n) \leq \sum m(\Omega_n) < \infty$), so
\[m(E) = m\!\left(\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty \bigcup_{n=N}^\infty \Omega_n\right) = \lim_{N\to\infty} m\!\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^\infty \Omega_n\right) = 0.\]
Hence almost every point belongs to only finitely many $\Omega_n$.

\medskip

\textbf{P5.} Let $p > 2$ and $c > 0$. Consider
\[E = \left\{x \in [0,1] : \left|x - \frac{a}{q}\right| \leq \frac{c}{q^p} \text{ for infinitely many } a, q \in \N\right\}.\]
For each $q \in \N$, the condition $0 \leq a \leq q$ means there are $q+1$ choices of $a$. For each pair $(a,q)$, define
\[\Omega_{a,q} = \left\{x \in [0,1] : \left|x - \frac{a}{q}\right| \leq \frac{c}{q^p}\right\}.\]
Then $\Omega_{a,q} \subseteq [0,1]$ is an interval of length $2c/q^p$, so $m(\Omega_{a,q}) = 2c/q^p$. The set $E$ is contained in
\[\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty \bigcup_{q=N}^\infty \bigcup_{a=0}^q \Omega_{a,q}.\]
For each fixed $q$, there are $q+1$ intervals $\Omega_{a,q}$, each of measure $2c/q^p$, so
\[\sum_{a=0}^q m(\Omega_{a,q}) = \frac{2c(q+1)}{q^p}.\]
Summing over all $q \geq 1$:
\[\sum_{q=1}^\infty \frac{2c(q+1)}{q^p} = 2c \sum_{q=1}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{q^{p-1}} + \frac{1}{q^p}\right) < \infty\]
since $p > 2$ implies both $p-1 > 1$ and $p > 1$. By the Borel--Cantelli lemma (P4), $m(E) = 0$.

\medskip

\textbf{P6.} Let $f: \Omega \to \R^*$ be absolutely integrable, so $\int_\Omega |f| < \infty$. By definition, $\int_\Omega f = \int_\Omega f^+ - \int_\Omega f^-$, where $f^+ = \max(f,0) \geq 0$, $f^- = -\min(f,0) \geq 0$, and $|f| = f^+ + f^-$. Since all three are non-negative measurable functions with finite integrals:
\[|\int_\Omega f| = \left|\int_\Omega f^+ - \int_\Omega f^-\right| \leq \int_\Omega f^+ + \int_\Omega f^- = \int_\Omega (f^+ + f^-) = \int_\Omega |f|.\]

\medskip

\textbf{P7.} Let $f, g: \Omega \to \R$ be absolutely integrable.

\medskip
\noindent(a) \emph{Scalar multiplication:} If $c = 0$, the result is trivial. If $c \neq 0$, then $(cf)^+ = \max(cf,0) = c f^+$ if $c > 0$ and $(cf)^+ = |c| f^-$ if $c < 0$ (and similarly for $(cf)^-$). In either case, $\int |cf| = |c| \int |f| < \infty$, and $\int cf = c \int f$ follows from linearity on $f^+$ and $f^-$.

\medskip
\noindent(b) \emph{Addition:} Since $|f+g| \leq |f| + |g|$ pointwise, we have $\int |f+g| \leq \int |f| + \int |g| < \infty$, so $f+g \in L^1$. Write $f+g = (f+g)^+ - (f+g)^-$. One can show (by checking the definitions of $+$ and $-$ on each region $\{f > g\}$, $\{f < g\}$, etc.) that $(f+g)^+ - (f+g)^- = f^+ - f^- + g^+ - g^-$. Integrating both sides and rearranging gives
\[(f+g)^+ + f^- + g^- = (f+g)^- + f^+ + g^+.\]
Since all terms are non-negative and all integrals are finite, integrating yields
\[\int (f+g)^+ + \int f^- + \int g^- = \int (f+g)^- + \int f^+ + \int g^+,\]
which rearranges to $\int (f+g) = \int f + \int g$.

\medskip
\noindent(c) \emph{Monotonicity:} If $f(x) \leq g(x)$ for all $x$, then $g - f \geq 0$ pointwise. By non-negativity of the integral (Proposition 8.1.10 in Tao), $\int (g-f) \geq 0$. Using linearity from (b), $\int g - \int f = \int (g-f) \geq 0$, so $\int f \leq \int g$.

\medskip
\noindent(d) \emph{Almost everywhere equality:} If $f = g$ a.e., let $E = \{x: f(x) \neq g(x)\}$. Then $m(E) = 0$. Since $f = g$ on $\Omega \setminus E$,
\[\int_\Omega f = \int_{\Omega \setminus E} f + \int_E f = \int_{\Omega \setminus E} g + \int_E g = \int_\Omega g,\]
because $m(E) = 0$ implies $\int_E f = \int_E g = 0$.

why only has to consider those eintegers a in the range 0 <= a <= p
</user_query>

Because intervals outside $0 \le a \le q$ don't intersect $[0,1]$ at all.

For any $a > q$, we have $a/q > 1$. The interval
$$\left[\frac{a}{q} - \frac{c}{q^p},\; \frac{a}{q} + \frac{c}{q^p}\right]$$
has lower bound $> 1$ (since even the lower bound exceeds $1$), so it lies **entirely outside** $[0,1]$. Similarly, for $a < 0$, the interval lies entirely below $0$.

Thus for $x \in [0,1]$, the condition $|x - a/q| \le c/q^p$ can only possibly be satisfied when $0 \le a/q \le 1$, i.e., $0 \le a \le q$.

\textbf{Defs:}\par

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Continuity (7.9):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ cont at $x_0\in E$ $\implies f$ cont at $x_0$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Integrability (7.10):} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$, each integrable $\implies f$ integrable and $\int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Cauchy Criterion (7.11):} $f_n$ conv uniformly on $E$ $\iff\forall\varepsilon>0$, $\exists N:n,m\ge N\implies|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon\ \forall x\in E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform $\Rightarrow$ Differentiability (7.12):} (1) $(a,b)$ bounded; (2) each $f_n$ diff on $(a,b)$; (3) $f_n(x_0)\to L$ for some $x_0$; (4) $f_n'$ converges uniformly on $(a,b)$ $\implies$ $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $(a,b)$ and $f'=\lim f_n'$.\smallskip

\textbf{Product of Uniformly Conv Functions:} If $f_n\to f$, $g_n\to g$ uniformly on $E$ and $f,g$ bounded on $E$, then $f_ng_n\to fg$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Arith. Mean Conv:} $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, each $f_n$ bounded $\implies$ $\frac{f_1+\dots+f_n}{n}\to f$ uniformly on $E$.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniqueness (7.39):} If $f(x)=\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ on open interval $I$, then $a_k=f^{(k)}(x_0)/k!$. Hence analytic $\implies C^\infty$.\smallskip

\textbf{Analytic (7.38):} $f$ analytic on open interval $I$ $\iff$ $\forall x_0\in I$, $\exists$ power series $\sum a_k(x-x_0)^k$ converging to $f$ near $x_0$. Equivalently: the Taylor series at each $x_0$ converges to $f$ in a neighborhood.\smallskip

\textbf{Analytic characterizations:}\par
\nobreak\smallskip\noindent (1) Remainder criterion: $f\in C^\infty$, $R_n(x)=f(x)-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f^{(k)}(x_0)/k!(x-x_0)^k$, then $f$ analytic $\iff$ $R_n(x)\to0$ near every $x_0$. (2) Growth condition (7.43): $|f^{(n)}(x)|\le M^n$ for all $n,x$ $\implies$ analytic (e.g. $e^x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ are analytic on $\mathbb R$). (3) Taylor conv $\iff$ analytic: $C^\infty$ + Taylor series converges to $f$ on open interval $\iff$ $f$ analytic. (4) Analytic $\iff$ $f'$ analytic (Ex 7.4.8). (5) Analytic continuation (7.56): if $f,g$ analytic on $I,J$ and agree on a nontrivial subinterval, then $f=g$ on $I\cap J$.\smallskip

\textbf{Counterexample (7.41):} $f(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x\neq0$, $f(0)=0$: $f\in C^\infty$, all $f^{(n)}(0)=0$, so Taylor series is identically $0\neq f(x)$ for $x\neq0$. So $C^\infty\not\Rightarrow$ analytic.\smallskip

\textbf{Uniform Boundedness + Conv $\Rightarrow$ Bounded:} $f_n$ uniformly bounded on $E$ + $f_n\to f$ uniformly $\implies f$ bounded on $E$.\smallskip
